chapters.title: Air, Pressure and the Shape of a Wing

sections.title: 1.7 The aerodynamic force on an aerofoil

chapters.html:
Principles of flight starts with the air itself: what it weighs, how its pressure and density change, and how energy is traded between pressure and speed as it flows. From that come the airspeeds a pilot reads and the words used to describe an aerofoil and a wing. Everything later in the subject, lift, drag, stalls and stability, is built on these definitions.

1.1 Units, mass and Newton's laws

The exam uses SI units throughout. 01.01.01.01

Key numbers · SI units

Quantity SI unit
Mass kilogram (kg)
Acceleration metre per second squared (m/s²)
Force, weight newton (N = kg·m/s²)
Velocity metre per second (m/s)
Energy joule (J = N·m)
Power watt (W = J/s)
Density kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m³)
Temperature kelvin (K)
Pressure pascal (Pa = N/m²)
Wing loading newton per square metre (N/m²)

Mass is the amount of matter in a body and a measure of its resistance to acceleration (its inertia); it is the same everywhere. A force is what changes a body's state of rest or motion. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, in speed or in direction. Weight is the force of gravity on a mass: W = m × g, with g ≈ 9.81 m/s², so a 70 000 kg aeroplane weighs about 687 kN. 01.01.01.02

Newton's three laws describe how forces and motion are linked. 01.01.01.03

  1. A body stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless a resultant force acts on it. An aeroplane in steady, straight and level flight therefore has all its forces in balance.
  2. A resultant force produces an acceleration proportional to it and in its direction: F = m × a. Any change of speed or direction, including a turn, needs a resultant force.
  3. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. A wing pushes air downwards, and the air pushes the wing upwards; a propeller or jet accelerates air backwards and is pushed forwards.

1.2 Density, pressure and temperature

Air density (ρ, rho) is the mass of air per unit volume, about 1.225 kg/m³ at sea level in ISA. Aerodynamic forces depend directly on it, because a wing makes its force by changing the momentum of the air it meets. 01.01.01.04

Density is set by pressure, temperature and humidity. 01.01.01.05 Higher pressure packs more molecules into a volume, so density rises with pressure; higher temperature spreads them out, so density falls with temperature. Humid air is slightly less dense than dry air, because water vapour molecules are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen they replace. Climbing, pressure falls faster than temperature, so density falls with altitude: at about 22 000 ft it is half its sea-level value. 01.01.01.06

The three are linked by the equation of state for a perfect gas, p = ρ × R × T, with T in kelvin and R the gas constant for air (287 J/kg/K). At constant pressure, density is inversely proportional to absolute temperature; at constant temperature, it is proportional to pressure. 01.01.01.15

Exam trap. A hot, high, humid day gives the lowest density and the poorest performance. Remember to use kelvin in the gas law: 15 °C is 288 K.

1.3 Static, dynamic and total pressure

Static pressure (p) is the pressure the air exerts on a surface moving with it, acting equally in all directions; it is the pressure of the still atmosphere. 01.01.01.07

Dynamic pressure (q) is the pressure the air would add if it were brought to rest: the kinetic energy of the flow per unit volume. 01.01.01.08 Its formula is

q = ½ ρ V²

with ρ the density and V the true airspeed. 01.01.01.09 Dynamic pressure is what a wing actually feels: lift, drag, control forces and structural loads all scale with it. It is also what the airspeed indicator measures, so IAS is a measure of dynamic pressure. The same IAS means the same q, and so the same aerodynamic forces at the same angle of attack, at any altitude; at altitude, where ρ is lower, a higher TAS is needed to make that q. 01.01.01.10

For steady, incompressible flow without friction, Bernoulli's equation says that along a streamline

p + ½ ρ V² = constant = total pressure (pT)

So where the air speeds up its static pressure falls, and where it slows down its static pressure rises: energy is traded between pressure and motion, but the total stays the same. 01.01.01.11

Total pressure is static plus dynamic pressure, the pressure measured where the flow is brought fully to rest, as in a pitot tube. It is constant only within one system of flow. Energy added or removed changes it: total pressure rises through a propeller disc or a compressor, and falls through friction in a boundary layer, in a wake or across a shock wave. So the total pressure behind a propeller is not the same as in the free stream around it. 01.01.01.12

1.4 Continuity and the venturi

The equation of continuity says that in steady flow the mass passing every cross-section of a stream tube per second is the same: ρ × A × V = constant. In incompressible flow ρ is constant, so A × V = constant: where the tube narrows the air speeds up, and where it widens it slows down. 01.01.01.16

Combine continuity with Bernoulli in a venturi, a tube that narrows to a throat and widens again. At the throat the area is smallest, so the speed is highest and the static pressure lowest; downstream the speed and pressure return to their entry values (ignoring friction). The total pressure is the same all the way through. A wing does something similar: the curved upper surface narrows the stream tubes above it, speeding the air up and lowering its pressure. 01.01.01.13

Worked example · continuity. Air enters a venturi at 50 m/s through 0.2 m². At a throat of 0.1 m² it flows at 50 × 0.2 / 0.1 = 100 m/s. Dynamic pressure rises from ½ × 1.225 × 50² ≈ 1531 Pa to ½ × 1.225 × 100² ≈ 6125 Pa, so the static pressure at the throat is about 4594 Pa lower.

1.5 From pitot-static pressures to airspeeds

The pitot tube faces the airflow and senses total pressure; the static ports sense static pressure. The airspeed indicator subtracts one from the other, pT − p = q, and is calibrated to show the speed that would give that q at ISA sea-level density. That reading is the indicated airspeed. 01.01.01.14

The four airspeeds then follow one another. 01.01.01.17

  • IAS (indicated airspeed): the instrument reading.
  • CAS (calibrated airspeed): IAS corrected for instrument error and position (pressure) error.
  • EAS (equivalent airspeed): CAS corrected for compressibility. EAS fixes the dynamic pressure exactly: q = ½ ρ0 EAS². At low speed and altitude CAS ≈ EAS.
  • TAS (true airspeed): the real speed through the air, EAS × √(ρ0 / ρ). At altitude TAS is well above EAS.

1.6 Airflow, streamlines and stream tubes

Flow is steady when the speed, pressure and direction at every fixed point stay the same with time; it is unsteady when they change, as in a gust, behind a stalled wing, or in a wake. 01.01.02.01

A streamline is a line drawn so that it is everywhere parallel to the local flow; in steady flow it is also the path of each particle. Because flow is along streamlines, none crosses them. A bundle of streamlines forms a stream tube, whose walls no air crosses either. 01.01.02.02 Air in a stream tube behaves as if it were in a pipe: where the streamlines converge the tube narrows and the air speeds up with a fall in static pressure; where they diverge it slows down and the pressure rises (continuity and Bernoulli together). 01.01.02.03

Two-dimensional flow is flow around a wing section of infinite span, the same in every slice, with no flow along the span. It describes an aerofoil. Three-dimensional flow is flow around a real wing of finite span, where air leaks round the tips, flows spanwise and forms tip vortices; it adds induced drag and changes the lift (Chapter 3). 01.01.02.04

1.7 The aerodynamic force on an aerofoil

The air presses on every part of an aerofoil's surface and drags along it. Added up, these pressures and frictions give one resultant aerodynamic force, acting at a point on the chord line called the centre of pressure (CP). It points upwards and inclined backwards. 01.01.03.01

The resultant is split into two components. Lift is the component perpendicular to the relative airflow (the undisturbed flow far ahead of the wing); drag is the component parallel to it, in the direction of the flow. 01.01.03.02 Lift is therefore not necessarily vertical: it is at right angles to the flight path, and in a climb or a turn it tilts with it. Drag always acts directly opposite to the flight path through the air. 01.01.03.03

The angle of attack (α, alpha) of an aerofoil is the angle between its chord line and the relative airflow. 01.01.03.08

Because the CP moves as the angle of attack changes, it is easier to place the lift and drag at a fixed point and add a pitching (aerodynamic) moment that does not change with angle of attack. That point is the aerodynamic centre (AC), about a quarter of the chord back from the leading edge in subsonic flow. The aerodynamic moment is the twisting moment of the aerodynamic force about the AC, and depends on the camber of the section, the dynamic pressure, and the wing's area and chord: M = CM × q × S × c. 01.01.03.04–05

On a symmetrical aerofoil the CP stays at the AC, so the moment about the AC is zero. 01.01.03.06 A positively cambered aerofoil has a nose-down moment about the AC, constant with angle of attack; a negatively cambered one has a nose-up moment. 01.01.03.07

1.8 The aerofoil section

The leading edge is the front of the section, the first part to meet the air, and the trailing edge the sharp rear edge where the upper and lower flows meet. 01.01.04.01–02 The chord line is the straight line joining the two; its length is the chord. 01.01.04.03

The thickness-to-chord ratio (relative thickness) is the maximum thickness divided by the chord, as a percentage: around 12 % for a typical subsonic wing, less for high-speed wings. 01.01.04.04 The location of maximum thickness is given as a percentage of the chord from the leading edge; further aft favours laminar flow and higher critical Mach numbers. 01.01.04.05

The camber line (mean line) runs midway between the upper and lower surfaces from leading to trailing edge. 01.01.04.06 Camber is the greatest distance between the camber line and the chord line, again as a percentage of chord. 01.01.04.07 The nose radius (leading-edge radius) describes how blunt the leading edge is: a large radius suits low speed and high lift, a sharp one suits high speed. 01.01.04.08

A symmetrical section has no camber: the camber line and chord line coincide, and it gives no lift at zero angle of attack. An asymmetrical (cambered) section has a curved camber line and gives lift even at zero angle of attack. 01.01.04.09

1.9 The wing

The span (b) is the tip-to-tip distance. 01.01.05.01 The root chord is the chord at the centreline, the tip chord the chord at the tip, and the taper ratio is tip chord ÷ root chord: 1 for a rectangular wing, 0 for a pointed delta. 01.01.05.02–03 The wing area (S) is the area of the planform projected onto a flat surface, normally including the part inside the fuselage. 01.01.05.04 The planform is the shape of the wing seen from above: rectangular, tapered, elliptical, swept or delta. 01.01.05.05

The mean geometric chord is simply the area divided by the span, S / b. 01.01.05.06 The mean aerodynamic chord (MAC) is the chord of an imaginary rectangular wing that would have the same aerodynamic forces and moments as the real one; the CG position and its limits are given as a percentage of the MAC. 01.01.05.07

The aspect ratio (A) is span ÷ mean chord, or b² / S. A long, slender wing has a high aspect ratio (a glider about 25, an airliner about 9), a short stubby one a low one. 01.01.05.08

The dihedral angle is the upward angle of the wing from the root to the tip, seen from the front; a downward angle is anhedral. 01.01.05.09 The sweep angle is the angle between a spanwise line on the wing, usually the quarter-chord line, and the lateral axis. 01.01.05.10

Wing twist varies the angle of attack along the span. Geometric twist (washout) reduces the angle of incidence of the sections from root to tip; aerodynamic twist does the same by changing the section shape, using less camber or a section with a lower zero-lift angle towards the tip. Both make the root stall before the tip (Chapter 7). 01.01.05.11

The angle of incidence is the angle between the aeroplane's longitudinal axis and the wing-root chord line. It is fixed when the aeroplane is built. Some older books use "angle of incidence" for angle of attack; for the EASA exam they are different things. 01.01.05.12

Worked example · aspect ratio. A wing of 34 m span and 122 m² area has A = 34² / 122 = 1156 / 122 ≈ 9.5. Its mean geometric chord is 122 / 34 ≈ 3.6 m.

Check yourself

  1. What happens to air density if the temperature rises at constant pressure? It falls, in inverse proportion to the absolute temperature.
  2. Write Bernoulli's equation and say what it means for a wing. p + ½ρV² = constant: where the air over the wing speeds up, its static pressure falls.
  3. Which airspeed fixes the dynamic pressure exactly? EAS: q = ½ρ0 EAS².
  4. A stream tube narrows from 3 m² to 1 m². What happens to the speed in incompressible flow? It triples.
  5. Where does the aerodynamic centre lie, and what is special about it? At about 25 % of the chord; the pitching moment about it does not change with angle of attack.
  6. Which way does a positively cambered aerofoil pitch about its AC? Nose-down.
  7. Define the angle of incidence for the EASA exam. The angle between the longitudinal axis and the wing-root chord line.
  8. A wing has a span of 11 m and an area of 16.2 m². What is its aspect ratio? About 7.5.

2.6 Lift and the angle of attack

chapters.html:
This chapter follows the air around a wing section: where it splits, where it speeds up, how the pressure falls on top and rises underneath, and how that pressure field becomes lift, drag and a pitching moment. It ends with the coefficients that let one formula describe any wing at any speed, and with the lift curve, the single most useful graph in the subject.

2.1 The streamline pattern

Seen from the wing, the air approaches in parallel streamlines. Ahead of the leading edge they start to curve upwards, which is called upwash. They divide at the leading edge, pass over and under the section, and leave the trailing edge deflected downwards, which is called downwash. Over the curved upper surface the streamlines are squeezed together; under the lower surface they stay further apart. 01.02.01.01 01.02.01.03

Where streamlines converge, the stream tube narrows, so by continuity the air speeds up and by Bernoulli its static pressure falls. Where they diverge, the air slows down and its pressure rises. Over the front of the upper surface the streamlines converge strongly; towards the trailing edge they diverge again. 01.02.01.02

2.2 The stagnation point

The streamline that divides the flow going over the wing from the flow going under it meets the leading edge at the stagnation point. There the air is brought to rest, its speed is zero and its static pressure is the highest anywhere on the section: it equals the total pressure, with a pressure coefficient of +1. 01.02.02.01

As the angle of attack increases, the stagnation point moves down and back along the lower surface of the leading edge. More of the air then has to go round the nose to reach the upper surface, and the suction peak just behind the leading edge becomes sharper. As the angle of attack decreases, the stagnation point moves up towards the nose, and at negative angles onto the upper surface. 01.02.02.02

2.3 Pressure distribution

The air over the upper surface moves faster than the free stream and has a lower static pressure, which acts as suction. Under the lower surface at positive angles of attack the air moves a little slower and the pressure is slightly above ambient. Lift is the sum of the pressure difference between the two surfaces, and at normal angles of attack roughly two-thirds of it comes from the suction on top. The suction is greatest a short way behind the leading edge, the suction peak, and decreases towards the trailing edge, where the two surfaces return to about ambient pressure. 01.02.03.01

Increasing the angle of attack strengthens the suction peak and moves it forward, and raises the pressure under the lower surface. Adding camber spreads the suction along more of the chord and increases the lift at any angle of attack, so a cambered section gives lift even at zero angle of attack, while a symmetrical one gives none there.

2.4 Centre of pressure and aerodynamic centre

The centre of pressure (CP) is where the resultant aerodynamic force acts: the point about which the pressure distribution has no moment. On a cambered section it moves as the angle of attack changes. As the angle of attack increases, the suction peak moves forward and the CP moves forward, towards about 25–30 % of the chord, until the stall, when it moves back sharply. At small angles of attack the CP of a cambered wing is far aft. That movement makes the CP awkward for stability work.

The aerodynamic centre (AC) is the fixed point, about 25 % of the chord in subsonic flow, about which the pitching moment stays constant as the angle of attack changes. Lift changes act at the AC, and the constant camber moment is added to them. For a symmetrical section the AC and CP coincide. 01.02.04.01

Exam trap. The CP moves; the AC does not. For a positively cambered aerofoil the CP moves forward as the angle of attack increases, up to the stall.

2.5 Drag and the wake

Two physical phenomena cause the drag of an aerofoil: friction in the thin layer of air next to the surface, and the pressure difference between the front and back of the body. 01.02.06.01

Skin friction drag is caused by the viscosity of the air: in the boundary layer the air is slowed down by the surface, and the surface is dragged backwards in return. It depends on the wetted area, the surface roughness and whether the boundary layer is laminar or turbulent; a turbulent boundary layer has much higher friction. 01.02.06.02

Form (pressure) drag arises because the flow does not fully recover its pressure at the back of the body. The boundary layer thickens and may separate, leaving a low-pressure region behind; the higher pressure on the front then pushes the body backwards. It depends on the shape: blunt bodies with separated flow have high form drag, streamlined bodies low. 01.02.06.03

Both appear as a wake: a region of slowed-down, often turbulent air trailing the body. The air in the wake has lost speed, so it has lost momentum; by Newton's laws the force that took that momentum out of the air is the drag. The energy that the engines must supply to overcome drag ends up as the motion and heat of the wake. 01.02.06.04

2.6 Lift and the angle of attack

As the angle of attack increases from small values, the flow is turned more strongly, the suction on top deepens and the pressure underneath rises, so the lift increases, almost in proportion. This continues up to a point where the air can no longer follow the upper surface: the flow separates, and lift stops increasing and then falls (the stall, Chapter 7). 01.02.07.01

2.7 The lift curve

The CL–α graph (the lift curve) plots the lift coefficient against the angle of attack. Over most of its range it is a straight line; near the top it curves over to a maximum and then drops away. 01.02.09.01

Three points on it matter. 01.02.09.02

  • Where the curve crosses the horizontal axis, CL = 0: the zero-lift angle of attack. It is 0° for a symmetrical section and negative (about −2° to −4°) for a positively cambered one.
  • Where the curve crosses the vertical axis, α = 0: the lift coefficient at zero angle of attack. It is zero for a symmetrical section and positive for a cambered one.
  • The maximum of the curve: CLMAX, reached at the critical angle of attack (αCRIT, the stalling angle), typically 15–20° for a wing without high-lift devices.

2.8 Why coefficients

The force on a wing depends on its size, the air density, the speed and its shape and angle of attack. Coefficients separate the part that depends only on shape and angle of attack from the rest. A coefficient is a dimensionless number: the force divided by the dynamic pressure and the wing area. Once it is known for a shape, the force can be worked out for any size, speed and density, and results from a wind tunnel model apply to the full-size aeroplane. 01.03.01.01

2.9 The lift formula

L = CL × ½ ρ V² × S

Lift is the lift coefficient times the dynamic pressure times the wing area. So lift is proportional to the density, to the square of the TAS (or simply to the square of the EAS, since ½ρV² = ½ρ0 EAS²), to the wing area and to the lift coefficient, which depends on the angle of attack and the shape. Doubling the speed at the same angle of attack gives four times the lift. 01.03.02.01

Worked example · lift. A wing of 30 m² at CL 0.5 flies at 60 m/s TAS at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³). L = 0.5 × ½ × 1.225 × 60² × 30 = 0.5 × 2205 × 30 ≈ 33 kN, enough to hold up a mass of about 3370 kg.

CL depends in low subsonic flight on the angle of attack, the shape of the section (camber, thickness, nose radius), the planform and aspect ratio, the configuration (flaps and slats), and the state of the surface (contamination, ice). It is not affected by speed or density as such, which already appear in the formula, except through Mach number effects at high speed (Chapter 6). 01.03.02.05

Camber shifts the lift curve. A symmetrical section's curve passes through the origin. A positively cambered section's curve is moved up and to the left: it gives lift at zero angle of attack, its zero-lift angle is negative, and its CLMAX is usually somewhat higher. A negatively cambered section's curve is moved down and to the right. The slope stays about the same. 01.03.02.02

A fast aerofoil, thin and with little camber and a sharp nose, has a lower CLMAX and stalls at a lower angle of attack, often abruptly. A slow aerofoil, thicker, more cambered and with a larger nose radius, has a higher CLMAX at a higher stalling angle and a gentler stall. 01.03.02.03

CLMAX is the highest lift coefficient the wing can reach; αCRIT is the angle of attack at which it occurs. Beyond αCRIT the lift coefficient falls: the wing has stalled. 01.03.02.04

2.10 The drag formula

Drag follows the same pattern:

D = CD × ½ ρ V² × S

with CD the drag coefficient, depending on shape, angle of attack and surface. For a two-dimensional section, CD is made up of friction and form drag (the profile drag), and at a given CD drag is proportional to the dynamic pressure. 01.03.03.01

The drag coefficient of a body depends strongly on its shape: a flat plate across the flow has a CD of about 1.2, a sphere about 0.5, and a streamlined body only about 0.05 for the same frontal area. A larger cross-sectional (frontal) area gives more drag for the same CD, which is why drag coefficients must always say which reference area they use. A rough surface makes the boundary layer turbulent earlier and raises the friction drag. 01.03.03.02

Check yourself

  1. Where on the section is the static pressure highest? At the stagnation point, where the air is brought to rest.
  2. Which way does the stagnation point move as the angle of attack increases? Down and back, along the lower surface of the leading edge.
  3. Which surface gives most of the lift? The upper surface, through suction.
  4. What are the two physical causes of drag? Friction in the boundary layer, and pressure (form) differences between the front and back.
  5. What does camber do to the lift curve? Moves it up and to the left: lift at zero angle of attack and a negative zero-lift angle, with about the same slope.
  6. Speed doubles at the same angle of attack and density. What happens to lift? It increases four times.
  7. Which kind of aerofoil has the higher CLMAX, thick and cambered or thin and symmetrical? Thick and cambered.

sections.title: 3.1 Angle of attack and attitude in three dimensions

chapters.html:
A real wing has tips. At the tips the high-pressure air underneath leaks round to the low-pressure air on top, and that small leak reshapes the whole flow: it rolls up into tip vortices, tilts the airflow down behind the wing, adds a drag that gets worse the slower the aeroplane flies, and leaves a wake that can upset a following aircraft. This chapter follows that chain and ends with the drag polar, which sums up a wing's efficiency.

3.1 Angle of attack and attitude in three dimensions

For a whole aeroplane, the angle of attack is the angle between the longitudinal axis and the relative airflow (for a wing section it was the chord line). 01.04.01.01

The attitude (pitch angle) is the angle between the longitudinal axis and the horizon. They are different things. In level flight the flight path is horizontal, so the attitude and the angle of attack are the same. In a climb the attitude equals the angle of attack plus the climb angle; in a glide the nose can be below the horizon while the angle of attack is positive. A wing can stall at any attitude. 01.04.01.02

3.2 Spanwise flow and tip vortices

Seen from above, the air over the wing does not flow straight back. Under the wing the pressure is higher than ambient, so the air there drifts outwards towards the tips; over the wing it is lower, so the air drifts inwards towards the root. At the tips the high-pressure air flows round from below to the low-pressure side above. 01.04.02.01–02

Where the upper and lower flows meet at the trailing edge they cross at a small angle and form a sheet of small vortices, which rolls up into two strong wing-tip vortices just behind and inboard of the tips. Seen from behind, the left vortex turns clockwise and the right one anticlockwise: both rise outboard of the tips and sink inboard. Together they push the air behind the wing downwards; this adds to the downwash behind the wing. 01.04.02.03

The strength of the vortices depends on the pressure difference between the surfaces, so on the lift coefficient. At high angles of attack (low speed, high weight, steep turns), CL is high and the vortices are strong; at high speed and low angle of attack they are weak. 01.04.02.04

3.3 Spanwise lift distribution

Lift is not the same all along the span. It falls to zero at the tips, where the pressures equalise. An elliptical planform (or an equivalent mix of taper and twist) gives an elliptical lift distribution with a uniform downwash, which produces the least induced drag for a given span. A rectangular wing carries relatively more lift near the tips than the ideal and its root sections work harder; a highly tapered or swept wing carries relatively more lift outboard. That distribution also decides where the stall begins (Chapter 7). 01.04.02.05

Extending flaps concentrates lift on the inner wing. The trailing vortices then form partly at the outboard ends of the flaps, and the tip vortices start further inboard; the effective span of the lifting system is reduced, so for the same lift the vortex wake is more concentrated. Flaps do not make the wake disappear. 01.04.02.07

3.4 Wake turbulence

The two vortices trail behind every aeroplane producing lift. Their strength depends on the aircraft's weight, speed and wingspan (and configuration): the strongest vortices come from an aeroplane that is heavy, clean and slow, as in the take-off climb and the approach. They start when the nosewheel lifts at rotation and stop when it touches down on landing. 01.04.02.08

Behind the aircraft the vortices sink at roughly 300–500 ft per minute, levelling off about 500–900 ft below the generating aircraft's flight path, and drift with the wind. Close to the ground they spread sideways at about 5 kt each; a light crosswind of 2–3 kt can hold the upwind vortex stationary over the runway. They decay slowly, typically lasting up to two or three minutes, longer in calm, stable air. The hazard to a following aeroplane is a strong induced roll, loss of height or structural load, worst when it flies straight along a vortex core. 01.04.02.06

Key numbers · wake vortices

Behaviour Typical value
Sink rate 300–500 ft/min
Levels off 500–900 ft below the flight path
Lateral spread near the ground ≈ 5 kt each way
Most dangerous crosswind 2–3 kt (holds a vortex over the runway)
Lifetime up to 2–3 min, longest in calm air

3.5 Induced drag

Behind the wing the downwash tilts the airflow down. The wing therefore meets air flowing slightly downwards, at a smaller effective angle of attack than its geometric angle of attack: the difference is the induced angle of attack. 01.04.03.07–08

Lift is perpendicular to the local, tilted airflow, so it is tilted backwards by the induced angle. Its component along the flight path is a drag force: induced drag. It is the price of making lift with a wing of finite span, and its root cause is the pressure difference that drives spanwise flow and the tip vortices. 01.04.03.01 01.04.03.09

The induced drag coefficient is approximately

CDi = CL² / (π × A × e)

so it grows with the square of the lift coefficient and falls with the aspect ratio A; e is an efficiency factor (1 for an ideal elliptical lift distribution, about 0.8 for a real aeroplane). 01.04.03.02 01.04.03.11

In straight and level flight the lift equals the weight, so the CL needed is high at low speed and low at high speed. Induced drag is therefore largest at low speed, falling roughly with 1/V² as speed rises; parasite drag does the opposite. At low speed induced drag is most of the total; at high speed it is a small part. 01.04.03.03

At a given IAS, more mass needs a higher CL, and induced drag grows with the square of the weight: 10 % more mass gives about 21 % more induced drag. 01.04.03.04

Taken together, induced drag depends on: 01.04.03.10

  • Speed: inversely proportional to the square of the speed.
  • Aspect ratio: inversely proportional to it. Long, slender wings have weaker vortices for the same lift.
  • Planform: least for an elliptical lift distribution; more for a rectangular or very tapered wing.
  • Bank angle in a level turn: the load factor n = 1/cos φ raises the lift needed, so induced drag grows with n². At 60° of bank (n = 2) it is four times as large.

A wing designer can reduce induced drag with: 01.04.03.05–06

  • a higher aspect ratio;
  • winglets, which recover some energy from the tip vortex and increase the effective span;
  • tip tanks, which act as end plates and slow the flow round the tip;
  • wing twist (washout), which shapes the lift distribution towards the ideal;
  • camber change along the span, which does the same;
  • in general, a lift distribution close to elliptical.

3.6 Induced drag on the graphs

Induced drag changes the lift curve of a three-dimensional wing. Because of the induced angle, a wing needs a larger geometric angle of attack to reach the same CL than an infinite wing would. The lift curve of a low-aspect-ratio wing is therefore less steep, and it reaches CLMAX at a higher angle of attack; a high-aspect-ratio wing has a steeper curve and stalls at a lower angle of attack. 01.04.03.12

The drag polar plots CL against CD (or CD against CL) for the whole aeroplane. For most aeroplanes it is close to a parabola:

CD = CDP + k × CL²

where CDP is the parasite drag coefficient, independent of lift, and k × CL² the induced drag, with k = 1/(πAe). A higher aspect ratio gives a smaller k and a polar that rises less steeply. 01.04.03.12–13

The point of minimum drag coefficient is where the curve is closest to the CL axis, at or near CL = 0. The more important point is where a straight line from the origin just touches the curve: there CL/CD is a maximum, which is the same as the best lift-to-drag ratio. The angle of attack at that point gives the least drag for the weight carried, the speed VMD (Chapter 4). 01.04.03.14

The L/D ratio measures aerodynamic efficiency: how much lift the aeroplane gets for each newton of drag. Its maximum fixes the best glide angle, the minimum thrust needed in level flight and, for a jet, the best endurance. A modern airliner reaches an L/D of about 17–20; a high-performance glider over 50. 01.04.03.15

Worked example · induced drag. A = 9, e = 0.8, CL = 0.5: CDi = 0.25 / (π × 9 × 0.8) = 0.25 / 22.6 ≈ 0.011. In a 60° turn at the same speed, CL doubles to 1.0 and CDi becomes about 0.044.

Check yourself

  1. Which way does the air flow along the lower surface of a wing? Outwards, towards the tips.
  2. Why are tip vortices strongest at low speed? Lift is the same but CL, and so the pressure difference between the surfaces, is highest.
  3. When is the wake of an airliner most dangerous? When it is heavy, clean and slow, after take-off and on approach.
  4. What tilts the lift vector backwards? The downwash, through the induced angle of attack.
  5. Mass increases by 20 % at the same IAS. What happens to induced drag? It rises by about 44 % (1.2²).
  6. Give the formula for the parabolic polar. CD = CDP + kCL².
  7. How do you find (L/D)max on a polar? Draw the tangent from the origin; the point where it touches the curve.
  8. Compare the lift curves of a high- and a low-aspect-ratio wing. The high-aspect-ratio wing's curve is steeper and reaches its CLMAX at a lower angle of attack.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: Total Drag, Speed and Ground Effect
chapters.html:
Drag comes in two families that behave in opposite ways: parasite drag grows with speed and induced drag shrinks. Their sum has a minimum, and that minimum, the speed VMD, organises much of what follows: speed stability, best glide, endurance. This chapter builds the drag curve, shows how weight and altitude move it, and then looks at what happens to the induced part close to the ground.

4.1 Parasite and induced drag

Total drag = parasite drag + induced drag. Parasite drag is all the drag that does not come from producing lift; induced drag is the drag caused by producing it. 01.05.01.01

Parasite drag itself has three parts. 01.05.02.01

  • Form (pressure) drag comes from the pressure difference between the front and the back of a body when the flow does not close smoothly behind it. It depends on the shape and the frontal area, and grows sharply if the flow separates; streamlining and fairings reduce it. 01.05.02.02
  • Interference drag appears where two parts meet, such as the wing and fuselage, a pylon and wing, or the tailplane and fin. Their boundary layers and pressure fields interact and the combined drag exceeds the sum of the separate drags. It depends on the angle between the surfaces and how the joint is shaped; fillets and fairings reduce it. 01.05.02.03
  • Friction drag is the shear in the boundary layer. It depends on the wetted area, the surface roughness (dirt, insects, rivets, paint, ice) and the proportion of laminar or turbulent boundary layer: a turbulent layer has several times the friction of a laminar one. 01.05.02.04

Parasite drag is proportional to the dynamic pressure, so at constant configuration it grows with the square of the speed (IAS or EAS): twice the speed gives four times the parasite drag. 01.05.03.01

4.2 The drag curve

Plotting drag against speed for an aeroplane in level flight at a given weight gives two opposite curves: parasite drag rising as V², induced drag falling as 1/V². Their sum, the total drag, is a U-shaped curve. 01.05.05.01

The bottom of that curve is the minimum drag speed, VMD. There parasite drag and induced drag are equal, and the aeroplane is flying at the angle of attack for (L/D)max. Flying faster, parasite drag dominates; flying slower, induced drag dominates. 01.05.05.02

Exam trap. VMD is where parasite and induced drag are equal, not where either one is smallest. It is also the speed for best L/D and best glide angle.

4.3 Weight and altitude

A heavier aeroplane needs more lift, so a higher CL at any speed and more induced drag. The whole curve moves up and to the right: the minimum drag is higher (proportional to the weight, since L/D at VMD is unchanged) and VMD is higher (proportional to √W). 01.05.07.01

Pressure altitude has a different effect depending on which speed is on the horizontal axis. Against IAS (more strictly EAS), the drag curve does not change with altitude, because drag depends on dynamic pressure, which a given EAS fixes. Against TAS, the curve moves to the right: the same drag is reached at a higher TAS in thinner air. VMD in TAS terms therefore increases with altitude, while VMD as an IAS stays the same. 01.05.07.02

4.4 Speed stability

The drag curve also shows how the aeroplane reacts to a small change of speed at a fixed thrust setting. 01.05.07.03–04

  • Above VMD (the front side of the drag curve), a speed decrease reduces drag. With thrust unchanged, the surplus thrust accelerates the aeroplane back to its original speed; a speed increase raises drag and slows it down again. This region is speed stable.
  • At VMD, drag hardly changes with a small change of speed: the speed is neutral, and it wanders.
  • Below VMD (the back side of the drag curve, or the region of reversed command), a speed decrease increases drag. With thrust unchanged, drag now exceeds thrust, so the aeroplane slows down further, and drag rises further. This region is speed unstable.

In the unstable region a small speed loss, from a gust or from raising the nose to correct a low glide path on approach, grows by itself. The aeroplane keeps decelerating towards the stall, or, if the pilot holds height, keeps needing more thrust. It typically happens at low speed and high weight, on a slow approach or a long, slow climb, and is the reason approach speeds are kept above VMD or flown with autothrust. 01.05.07.05

4.5 Ground effect

Within about one wingspan of the ground, and strongly within half a span, the ground gets in the way of the downwash and of the tip vortices. The vortices cannot develop fully, the downwash behind the wing is reduced and the airflow behind it is less deflected. 01.06.01.01

With less downwash, the induced angle of attack is smaller and the lift vector is tilted back less, so the induced drag coefficient falls. At a height of one-tenth of the span, CDi can be roughly halved. 01.06.01.02

So at a given geometric angle of attack the effective angle of attack is higher and the wing gives more lift (a higher CL). Seen on the lift curve, ground effect makes it steeper. 01.06.03.01

Because the effective angle of attack is higher, the wing reaches its critical angle at a lower geometric angle of attack: in ground effect αCRIT is reduced. 01.06.02.01

Entering ground effect, for example in the landing flare, the aeroplane experiences: 01.06.01.03

  • reduced induced drag, so it floats and loses speed slowly;
  • more lift at the same attitude;
  • reduced downwash at the tailplane, which increases its angle of attack and gives a nose-down pitching tendency;
  • a change in the static pressure at the static ports, which can make the airspeed indicator read differently.

Leaving ground effect after take-off reverses these: induced drag increases, the aeroplane needs a higher angle of attack for the same lift, it tends to pitch nose-up, and if it lifts off too early at too low a speed it may not be able to climb out of ground effect, or may sink back.

For take-off and landing, ground effect lets an aeroplane lift off at a lower speed than it could sustain in free air, which can lead to a premature lift-off and a sink after leaving ground effect; on landing it lengthens the float, especially if the approach speed is too high, and so the landing distance. 01.06.04.01

A low-wing aeroplane has its wing much closer to the ground, so it feels ground effect more strongly than a high-wing aeroplane: it floats more on landing and its take-off behaviour changes more. 01.06.04.02

4.6 Lift coefficient and speed

In steady, straight and level flight, lift equals weight: W = CL × ½ρV² × S. At a given weight and altitude, CL × V² is constant. Fly faster and CL must fall (lower angle of attack); fly slower and CL must rise. 01.07.01.01

Worked example · CL and speed. At 200 kt the aeroplane flies at CL 0.4. At 140 kt the same lift needs CL = 0.4 × (200/140)² = 0.4 × 2.04 ≈ 0.82. If CLMAX is 1.2, the stall speed is 200 × √(0.4/1.2) ≈ 115 kt.

Plotted, CL against speed is a curve falling steeply at low speed and flattening at high speed (CL ∝ 1/V²). Reading along it, any change in CL at a given weight means a change of speed: the minimum speed in level flight is where CL reaches CLMAX, the stall speed. 01.07.02.01

Check yourself

  1. What three drags make up parasite drag? Form (pressure), interference and friction drag.
  2. What happens to parasite drag when the IAS doubles? It increases four times.
  3. At VMD, how do parasite and induced drag compare? They are equal.
  4. How does a weight increase move the drag–speed curve? Up and to the right; VMD rises with √W.
  5. Does VMD as an IAS change with altitude? No; as a TAS it increases.
  6. You are below VMD on approach and the speed drops. Without a thrust change, what happens? Drag rises, so the speed keeps falling: the region is speed unstable.
  7. In ground effect, what happens to induced drag and to αCRIT? Induced drag falls; αCRIT is reduced.
  8. Which feels ground effect more, a low-wing or a high-wing aeroplane? The low-wing aeroplane.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: High-Lift Devices, Spoilers and Contamination
chapters.html:
A wing designed for efficient cruise has a modest CLMAX, which would make take-off and landing speeds unacceptably high. Flaps and slats raise CLMAX for the slow phases of flight; spoilers and speed brakes do the opposite, destroying lift or adding drag when the pilot needs to slow down or descend. This chapter also covers what ice, dirt and age do to a wing.

5.1 Trailing-edge flaps

There are four basic types of trailing-edge flap. 01.09.01.01

  • Plain flap: the rear of the wing hinges down. Simple, but it gives the smallest CLMAX increase and much drag at large deflections.
  • Split flap: only a plate on the lower surface hinges down, leaving the upper surface unchanged. A little more lift than a plain flap, and a lot of drag.
  • Slotted flap: the flap moves down and leaves a gap (slot) between it and the wing. High-energy air from below flows through the slot over the flap's upper surface, re-energising the boundary layer so the flow stays attached at larger deflections. Double and triple slotted flaps repeat the idea.
  • Fowler flap: the flap first slides back, increasing the wing area and chord, and then rotates down, usually with one or more slots. It gives the largest increase in CLMAX, with relatively little drag in the first stages, which suits take-off.

Lowering a flap increases the effective camber of the wing (and, for a Fowler flap, its area). More camber gives more lift at every angle of attack and a higher CLMAX, so the aeroplane can fly slower; it also gives more drag, which helps steepen the approach and slow the aeroplane down. Small flap settings give much lift for little drag (take-off); large settings give much drag for little extra lift (landing). 01.09.01.02

Flaps move the centre of pressure aft, because the extra lift is generated over the rear of the wing. On their own that produces a nose-down pitching moment; on a real aeroplane the change of downwash on the tailplane can reduce or reverse it, so the actual trim change depends on the type. Flaps reduce the stall speed, because CLMAX is higher. 01.09.01.03

On the lift curve, trailing-edge flaps move the curve up and to the left: at any angle of attack CL is higher; CLMAX is higher; αCRIT is a little lower; and a given CL is reached at a lower angle of attack. 01.09.01.04

On the polar, flaps move the curve to higher CL and higher CD; the maximum lift-to-drag ratio is lower than for the clean wing. 01.09.01.05 Because the glide angle is set by the L/D ratio, flaps make the glide steeper: useful on approach to come down steeply without gaining speed. 01.09.01.06

Flap asymmetry, one flap extended and the other not, or extended further, creates a strong rolling moment towards the side with less flap, plus some yaw. It may exceed the aileron's ability to correct, especially at low speed. Systems therefore compare left and right flap positions and stop the flaps if they disagree. 01.09.01.07

For take-off and landing, flaps give a lower stall speed, so lower take-off and landing speeds and shorter distances. Because they reach the needed CL at a lower angle of attack, the nose attitude is lower, which improves the pilot's view on approach and reduces the risk of a tail strike. 01.09.01.08

Flap-setting errors are dangerous. 01.09.01.09

  • Taking off with less flap than planned raises the real stall and rotation speeds above those used for planning: the take-off run is longer, rotation at the planned speed may not give lift-off, and the stall margin at V2 is reduced.
  • Taking off with more flap than planned shortens the run but reduces climb performance, which may not meet the obstacle gradient.
  • Retracting flaps too early or at too low a speed reduces CLMAX while the aeroplane is still slow: it may sink or meet the stall buffet. Retract on schedule at the minimum flap-retraction speeds.
  • Extending flaps late on approach leaves the aeroplane fast and high; extending too early, above VFE, risks structural damage.

5.2 Leading-edge devices

Leading-edge devices raise CLMAX mainly by letting the wing reach a higher angle of attack before the flow separates. 01.09.02.01

  • Slats are small aerofoils on the leading edge that move forward and down, opening a slot between them and the wing. They can be fixed, automatic (pulled out by the low pressure at high angle of attack) or powered.
  • Krueger flaps hinge down and forward from the lower surface of the leading edge, increasing camber and nose radius; they are often used on the inboard wing of swept-wing airliners.
  • Variable-camber flaps are leading-edge sections that flex or curve down, increasing the camber of the front of the wing.

The slot works by feeding high-energy air from the high-pressure area under the wing through a narrow, accelerating gap onto the upper surface. This energises the boundary layer and smooths the pressure distribution behind the leading edge, so the flow stays attached to a much higher angle of attack. 01.09.02.02

Leading-edge flaps (Krueger and variable camber) increase the effective camber at the front of the wing and its nose radius, which lets the air turn round the leading edge at high angles of attack without separating. 01.09.02.03

Leading-edge devices lower the stall speed, like trailing-edge flaps, but they do it by raising αCRIT rather than by raising the lift at a given angle of attack. Used together, as on almost every airliner, the two give the largest reduction in stall speed. 01.09.02.04

On the lift curve, slats extend the curve: the straight part continues to a higher CLMAX at a higher αCRIT; at normal angles of attack the curve is almost unchanged (slightly lower for a slat). Trailing-edge flaps, by contrast, shift the whole curve up and lower αCRIT. 01.09.02.05

On the polar, leading-edge devices add a little drag at low CL but extend the curve to higher CL; at high CL they can give less drag than the clean wing near its stall. 01.09.02.06

Slat asymmetry means one wing stalls at a lower angle of attack than the other. Near the stall the wing without slats stalls first and drops, creating a sharp roll and possibly a spin entry. 01.09.02.07

For take-off and landing, slats reduce speeds and distances because CLMAX is higher. Their disadvantage is that the high CL is reached at a high angle of attack, so the nose attitude is high: the pilot's view is worse and the tail is closer to the runway. That is why slats are combined with trailing-edge flaps. 01.09.02.08

Exam trap. Trailing-edge flaps: CLMAX up, αCRIT down, nose lower. Slats: CLMAX up, αCRIT up, nose higher.

5.3 Vortex generators

Vortex generators are rows of small vanes standing up from the surface, set at an angle to the flow. 01.09.03.01 Each one makes a small, strong vortex that mixes fast-moving air from outside the boundary layer down into it. The boundary layer gains energy and can then survive a stronger adverse pressure gradient before it separates. 01.09.03.02

They delay separation at high angles of attack, keep control surfaces effective, and, on high-speed wings, reduce shock-induced separation. Their cost is a small increase in parasite drag in cruise, and some extra weight and maintenance. 01.09.03.03

5.4 Spoilers

Spoilers are panels on the upper surface of the wing, ahead of the flaps, that hinge up into the airflow. They destroy part of the lift over the wing behind them and add drag. 01.10.01.01

  • Roll spoilers rise on one wing only, in step with the aileron on that side, to help roll the aeroplane (Chapter 9).
  • Flight spoilers (speed brakes) rise symmetrically in flight to increase drag and allow a faster descent or deceleration.
  • Ground spoilers (lift dumpers) rise fully on both wings after touchdown or in a rejected take-off. They dump the lift, putting the weight on the wheels so the brakes work, and add drag.

Spoilers move the lift curve down: at any angle of attack CL is lower, and CLMAX is reduced, so the stall speed rises. Using speed brakes close to the stall is therefore dangerous. 01.10.01.02 On the polar, spoilers reduce the lift and increase the drag, so the lift-drag ratio falls. 01.10.01.03

5.5 Speed brakes

Speed brakes are surfaces that add drag when needed: spoiler panels on the wing, or panels on the fuselage or tail cone. They are used to descend steeply without gaining speed, to slow down quickly (for example to meet an ATC speed restriction), and to manage energy on approach. 01.10.02.01

They increase parasite drag by adding form drag and causing separated flow behind them. 01.10.02.03 On the polar they move the curve to the right (more CD at every CL), so (L/D)max is lower. 01.10.02.02 Because parasite drag rises while induced drag is unchanged, the speed at which the two are equal, VMD, decreases. 01.10.02.04

With the extra drag, the aeroplane can descend at a steeper angle and a higher rate at the same speed, or descend at the same rate at a lower speed. 01.10.02.05

5.6 Ice and other contamination

In flight, ice builds up on parts that meet the airflow head-on and have small radii: the leading edges of the wings, tailplane and fin; engine intakes and propellers; probes, antennas and wipers; and on the windscreen. Thin, sharp surfaces such as the tailplane collect ice faster than the thick wing roots. 01.12.01.01

Even a thin layer of ice, frost or snow, with the roughness of coarse sandpaper, can change the aerodynamics drastically. 01.12.01.02

  • Lift: CLMAX falls, by up to about 30 % for frost or rough ice on the leading edge, more for large ridges.
  • Drag: increases, through roughness and the disturbed shape.
  • Stall speed: rises with the lower CLMAX, often by 15–20 % or more.
  • αCRIT: falls; the wing may stall before the stall warning, which is set for a clean wing, activates.
  • Stability and control: the tailplane may stall (Chapter 7); ailerons may become heavy or snatch; the aeroplane may become unstable.

At take-off these effects are worst, because the aeroplane is at high angle of attack close to the ground with no height to recover. Rotating at the normal speed with a contaminated wing can mean a stall, a wing drop or an inability to climb out of ground effect. That is why the clean wing concept applies: no take-off with frost, ice or snow adhering to critical surfaces. 01.12.01.03

5.7 Ageing aeroplanes

Over its life an airframe changes. Dents, distortion, poorly fitting panels, repairs with doublers and protruding fasteners, worn seals, mis-rigged control surfaces and extra antennas all add parasite drag and can produce small asymmetries that need constant trim. The result is higher fuel burn and lower performance, which operators allow for with performance (degradation) factors. 01.12.02.01

Roughness and steps on an older surface also make the boundary layer turn turbulent earlier and thicken, adding friction drag and making separation more likely, especially on laminar-flow surfaces. 01.12.02.02

Check yourself

  1. Which trailing-edge flap gives the largest CLMAX increase, and why? The Fowler flap: it increases both camber and wing area, usually with slots.
  2. What do trailing-edge flaps do to αCRIT and to the nose attitude on approach? They reduce αCRIT and give a lower nose attitude.
  3. How does a slot delay the stall? It feeds high-energy air from below onto the upper surface, energising the boundary layer.
  4. What happens to the stall speed when spoilers are raised? It increases, because CLMAX falls.
  5. Why does extending speed brakes lower VMD? Parasite drag rises while induced drag does not, so they become equal at a lower speed.
  6. What does frost on the leading edge do to αCRIT and the stall warning? αCRIT falls, so the wing may stall before the stall warning activates.
  7. You take off with less flap than planned. What can happen? Higher actual stall and lift-off speeds than planned: longer run, reduced stall margin, possible failure to lift off at the planned VR.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: High-Speed Flight
chapters.html:
Below about Mach 0.4 the air behaves as if it were incompressible. A jet cruises at Mach 0.78–0.85, where it is not: the air is squeezed as it flows round the wing, local flow becomes supersonic, shock waves form, and lift, drag, pitching moment and control effectiveness all change. This chapter explains why, and how swept, thin and supercritical wings put those effects off to a higher Mach number.

6.1 The speed of sound

The speed of sound is the speed at which a small pressure disturbance travels through the air. 02.01.01.01 It depends only on the air temperature:

a = √(γ R T), or in knots, a ≈ 38.95 √T (T in kelvin)

Warmer air carries sound faster. 02.01.01.03 In ISA it is about 661 kt at sea level (15 °C) and falls with the temperature as altitude increases, to about 573 kt at the tropopause (−56.5 °C, 36 089 ft). Above the tropopause, where the temperature is constant, it stays constant. 02.01.01.02

6.2 Mach number

The Mach number is the true airspeed divided by the local speed of sound: M = TAS / a. Mach 0.8 means flying at 80 % of the speed of sound in the air around the aeroplane. 02.01.02.01

At a constant flight level and CAS, the Mach number does not change with temperature. A warmer day raises the speed of sound, but it lowers the density at that pressure level, so the same CAS gives a higher TAS in the same proportion. Mach number is a function of the dynamic and static pressures only, which a given CAS and pressure altitude fix. 02.01.03.01

In a climb at constant IAS (CAS), TAS rises as density falls and the speed of sound falls with temperature, so the Mach number rises. In a climb at constant Mach number, TAS falls as the speed of sound falls (below the tropopause), and IAS falls faster. Because IAS is falling, the aeroplane needs a higher CL and so a higher angle of attack; at a given vertical speed the flight-path angle increases as TAS falls, and the pitch attitude (angle of attack plus flight-path angle) rises. The reverse happens in a descent. 02.01.03.02

Three risks follow. 02.01.03.03

  • Descending at constant Mach number, IAS increases steadily and may exceed VMO. Airliners therefore change from Mach to IAS at the crossover altitude in the descent.
  • Climbing at constant IAS, Mach number increases steadily and may exceed MMO. Hence the change from IAS to Mach at the crossover in the climb.
  • Climbing at too low a Mach number at high altitude, IAS becomes very low, the aeroplane flies at high CL, and it can approach the low-speed stall, made worse by compressibility lowering CLMAX.

6.3 Compressibility

At low speed the pressure changes around a wing are too small to change the air's density noticeably. From about Mach 0.4, in high subsonic flow, they are not: the density changes along a streamline. That is compressibility, and it continues through transonic and supersonic flight. 02.01.04.01 Mach number is the measure of how much compressibility matters. 02.01.04.03

Compressibility makes the pressure gradients round the wing, especially near the leading edge where the flow accelerates sharply, reach separation sooner at high angles of attack. The syllabus sums this up as compressibility worsening the pressure gradient and reducing CL overall; the clearest effect is a lower CLMAX. 02.01.04.02 Consequently the stall speed (as an IAS) is higher and αCRIT is lower at high Mach numbers than at low speed. 02.01.04.04

6.4 Flow regimes

The flow round an aeroplane is divided into four regimes. 02.01.05.01–02

  • Subsonic, below compressibility (below about M 0.4): density practically constant; the low-speed theory of the earlier chapters applies.
  • Subsonic, above compressibility (about M 0.4 up to MCRIT): the flow is subsonic everywhere, but density changes are significant; pressure coefficients and lift-curve slope increase with Mach number.
  • Transonic (from MCRIT to about M 1.3): the flow is mixed, partly subsonic and partly supersonic, with shock waves on the wing. Lift, drag and pitching moment change rapidly.
  • Supersonic (above about M 1.3): the flow is supersonic everywhere except in small regions, with shock waves at the nose and leading edges.

Many transport aeroplanes cruise slightly above MCRIT. A small, weak shock costs little drag, while the higher speed gives better productivity and, with a supercritical wing, a better specific range. They stay below the Mach number at which drag rises sharply. 02.01.05.03

6.5 Shock waves

A shock wave is a very thin region, a fraction of a millimetre thick, in which supersonic flow is slowed abruptly and its pressure, temperature and density jump. It forms where supersonic flow has to slow down or turn, and disturbances cannot travel ahead of it to warn the air. 02.02.01.01

Across a normal shock wave, one at right angles to the flow, the air changes as follows. 02.02.02.01

Key numbers · across a normal shock

Quantity Change
Velocity decreases (supersonic to subsonic)
Mach number decreases, to below 1
Static pressure increases
Static temperature increases
Density increases
Local speed of sound increases (temperature rises)
Total pressure decreases (energy lost)
Total temperature unchanged

On a wing, the normal shock stands roughly perpendicular to the surface, at the back of the region of supersonic flow above the wing. 02.02.02.02

As the Mach number increases at positive lift: 02.02.02.03

  • the supersonic region on the upper surface grows and the shock becomes stronger;
  • the shock moves aft towards the trailing edge;
  • a second shock appears on the lower surface, usually at a slightly higher Mach number, and also moves aft, often reaching the trailing edge first.

At a constant Mach number, increasing the angle of attack speeds up the flow over the upper surface: the upper shock becomes stronger and moves forward, while the lower-surface shock weakens. 02.02.02.04

6.6 The critical Mach number

The critical Mach number (MCRIT) is the free-stream Mach number at which the airflow somewhere on the aeroplane first reaches the local speed of sound (local Mach 1). Below it the flow is subsonic everywhere. 02.03.01.01

Anything that accelerates the flow over the wing more lowers MCRIT. 02.03.01.02

  • A higher angle of attack (higher CL) lowers it.
  • A higher weight needs more CL at the same speed and lowers it.
  • Manoeuvres with load factor above 1 need more CL and lower it.
  • A forward CG needs a larger down-load on the tail, so the wing must give more lift, and lowers it slightly; an aft CG raises it.

6.7 Lift above MCRIT

At constant angle of attack, CL first rises with Mach number above about M 0.4 (compressibility strengthens the suction), then, beyond MCRIT, the shock and shock-induced separation make it fall, and in supersonic flow it falls further. 02.03.02.01

Exceeding MCRIT therefore reduces both the CL at a given angle of attack and CLMAX, because shock-induced separation occurs at lower angles of attack than low-speed separation. 02.03.02.02

At high altitude a given IAS means a higher Mach number. CLMAX falls with Mach number, so the stall IAS rises with altitude. At low altitude the stall IAS is constant; at high altitude, the low-speed stall (or buffet) IAS increases, and the margin between the minimum and maximum speeds narrows (Chapter 7). 02.03.02.03 Shock-induced separation also makes αCRIT smaller at high Mach number. 02.03.02.04

A wing with a supercritical aerofoil is designed to fly above MCRIT with a weak shock. Exceeding MCRIT then brings several advantages: a higher cruise speed for little extra drag (a better speed-to-drag ratio), a better specific range (distance per unit of fuel, which depends on TAS × L/D), and a higher optimum altitude. 02.03.02.05

6.8 Drag above MCRIT

Wave drag is the extra drag caused by shock waves: energy lost in the shock itself, and the separation of the boundary layer it causes behind it (shock-induced separation). 02.03.03.01

At constant angle of attack, CD is nearly constant up to MCRIT, then rises slowly, then very steeply from the drag divergence Mach number (MDD), reaching a peak near Mach 1 before falling again in supersonic flow. 02.03.03.02 On the polar, increasing Mach number moves the curve to higher drag, with a lower maximum L/D, once the critical Mach number is exceeded. 02.03.03.03

Beyond MDD the aeroplane meets: 02.03.03.04

  • a steep drag rise, needing much more thrust for little extra speed;
  • instability, as shock positions on the two wings and the tail change;
  • Mach tuck, a nose-down pitching moment (Section 6.9);
  • a shock stall, the loss of lift caused by shock-induced separation, with buffet.

MDD is always higher than MCRIT: shocks first form at MCRIT, but the drag only rises sharply when they become strong enough to cause separation. For a typical airliner MDD is a few hundredths of a Mach number above MCRIT. 02.03.03.05

6.9 Pitching moment and Mach tuck

As the Mach number increases beyond MCRIT the shock moves aft, and the region of low pressure behind it grows towards the trailing edge, so the centre of pressure moves aft. 02.03.04.01 On a swept wing, shock-induced separation tends to begin near the roots, losing lift ahead of the CG while the tips, behind it, keep theirs; and the reduced downwash at the tail raises its angle of attack. Together they give a nose-down pitching moment that grows with Mach number: Mach tuck or tuck-under. If uncorrected, the aeroplane pitches down, speeds up, and the nose-down moment grows further. 02.03.04.02

To compensate, high-speed aeroplanes have a Mach trim system. 02.03.04.03 It senses the Mach number and adjusts the elevator or stabiliser trim nose-up automatically, in proportion to Mach number above a threshold, so the stick force gradient with speed stays positive and the pilot does not have to push less to fly faster. 02.03.04.04

If the Mach trim fails, the aeroplane flight manual imposes a lower maximum Mach number: the pilot reduces speed and stays below that limit, so that Mach tuck stays within the range where the natural stability is enough. 02.03.04.05

6.10 Controls at high Mach number

At high Mach number the shock wave on a wing or tailplane can sit ahead of the control surface. Behind the shock the flow is separated and the pressure changes made by deflecting the surface cannot travel forward through the shock. Control effectiveness is reduced, the surface can buzz or vibrate, and in extreme cases hinge moments reverse. That is one reason for all-moving tailplanes and spoilers on high-speed aeroplanes. 02.03.05.01

6.11 Raising MCRIT

Sweepback is the most powerful tool. A swept wing feels mainly the component of the airflow perpendicular to its quarter-chord line, V × cos Λ (Λ the sweep angle). The flow along the span does little to accelerate the air over the section. The wing behaves as if the Mach number were reduced by cos Λ, and it also looks thinner: the effective thickness-to-chord ratio is reduced because the chord measured along the flow is longer. MCRIT rises. 02.05.01.01

Worked example · sweep. At M 0.85 with 30° of sweep, the component perpendicular to the leading edge is 0.85 × cos 30° ≈ M 0.74. With 35° of sweep it would be about M 0.70.

Sweepback has a price at low speed. 02.05.01.02

  • The effective speed over the section is lower, so CLMAX is lower, and the lift curve is less steep.
  • High-lift devices are less efficient on a swept wing, but more are needed: airliners use powerful multiple-slotted flaps and slats.
  • Spanwise flow towards the tips thickens the boundary layer there, and the tips tend to stall first. The tips are behind the CG, so losing their lift gives a pitch-up, which drives the angle of attack further into the stall.

Sweep reduces wave drag at high subsonic speed by raising MCRIT and MDD. At low speed it slightly increases induced drag, because swept wings tend to have a lower effective aspect ratio and less efficient lift distribution. 02.05.01.03

Thin aerofoils with little camber accelerate the flow less over the upper surface, so the local Mach number stays lower and MCRIT is higher. Their cost is a lower CLMAX and a sharper stall, and less room for structure and fuel. 02.05.02.01

The supercritical aerofoil is designed to delay and weaken the shock. Its upper surface is flattened, so the flow accelerates only moderately and stays supersonic over a long, nearly constant region that ends in a weak shock well aft; much of the lift comes from aft camber (rear loading) on the lower surface. 02.05.02.02 Its advantages are a higher MDD for a given thickness, or a thicker wing for the same MDD (more room for fuel and structure, lighter, allowing less sweep or a higher aspect ratio), and less wave drag. Its disadvantages are a large nose-down pitching moment from the rear loading, which must be trimmed, a sensitivity to small changes in shape, and more complex manufacturing. 02.05.02.04

Vortex generators ahead of the shock position mix energetic air into the boundary layer, so it can withstand the sharp pressure rise across the shock without separating. They reduce shock-induced separation, buffet and control-surface buzz. 02.05.03.01

Check yourself

  1. What does the speed of sound depend on? Only the air temperature.
  2. At constant FL and CAS the temperature rises. What happens to Mach number? It stays the same.
  3. In a descent at constant Mach number, which limit is at risk? VMO, because IAS increases.
  4. Across a normal shock, what happens to static pressure, Mach number and total pressure? Static pressure rises; Mach number falls below 1; total pressure falls.
  5. Define MCRIT. The free-stream Mach number at which the local flow first reaches Mach 1 somewhere on the aeroplane.
  6. How does a heavier aeroplane affect MCRIT? Lowers it, because more CL is needed.
  7. Why does Mach tuck happen? The CP moves aft as the shock moves aft and separation starts near the roots, and downwash at the tail changes, giving a nose-down moment.
  8. Name the main advantage of a supercritical aerofoil. A higher drag-divergence Mach number for the same thickness (or a thicker wing for the same MDD).
