8.5 The neutral point and static margin

chapters.html:
An aeroplane is stable if, after a gust or a brief control input disturbs it, it tends to return to where it was without the pilot's help. That tendency is built into the design: the tailplane, the CG position, the fin, dihedral and sweep. This chapter separates the tendency to return (static stability) from the motion that follows (dynamic stability), and works through the three axes: pitch, yaw and roll, and how yaw and roll interact.

8.1 Static and dynamic stability

Imagine a ball. In a bowl it rolls back to the bottom when pushed: that is positive static stability. On a flat table it stays where it is put: neutral static stability. On top of an upturned bowl it rolls away: negative static stability (static instability). For an aeroplane, static stability is its initial tendency, immediately after a disturbance, to return to its original state of equilibrium. Aeroplanes are designed to be statically stable so that they hold their trimmed condition without constant correction and recover from gusts by themselves. 04.01.01.01

Manoeuvrability is the ease with which the aeroplane can be made to change its state, for example its attitude, flight path or load factor, and how quickly it responds to the controls. 04.01.01.02

The two pull in opposite directions. A very stable aeroplane resists being disturbed, including by its pilot: it needs large control forces and deflections to manoeuvre. A less stable aeroplane is more manoeuvrable but more demanding to fly steadily. Airliners are designed with moderate stability; aerobatic and fighter aircraft with little or none (fighters use computers to make up for it). 04.01.01.03

Dynamic stability describes the motion over time after the disturbance. If the motion dies away and the aeroplane settles back, it is dynamically stable (positive); if it continues at the same amplitude, neutral; if it grows, unstable (negative). The motion can be periodic (oscillating, swinging back and forth) or aperiodic (moving steadily one way, without oscillating). An aeroplane can be statically stable but dynamically unstable: it tends to return, but overshoots by more each time. Static stability is necessary for dynamic stability, but does not guarantee it. 04.01.01.04

8.2 Equilibrium

Stability can only be judged starting from equilibrium: the condition in which the sum of all forces and the sum of all moments on the aeroplane are zero, so it flies steadily without accelerating or rotating. 04.01.02.01

The forces in equilibrium are lift, weight, thrust and drag, plus any side force: in level flight lift balances weight and thrust balances drag. 04.01.03.01

The moments are about the three axes through the CG: pitching moments about the lateral axis, rolling moments about the longitudinal axis and yawing moments about the normal axis. 04.01.04.01 If the sum of the moments about an axis is not zero, the aeroplane starts to rotate about that axis, with an angular acceleration; trim, a stabiliser or a control deflection is then needed to restore the balance. 04.01.04.02

8.3 Balancing in pitch

The wing's lift acts at its centre of pressure (or, with the camber moment, at its aerodynamic centre), the weight at the CG. They are not at the same point, and the cambered wing has its own nose-down moment. The tailplane (stabiliser) provides the force that makes the sum of the pitching moments about the CG zero. 04.03.01.01

On a conventional aeroplane the CG is usually ahead of the wing's centre of pressure, so the wing's lift and camber moment pitch the nose down and the tailplane must push down (a negative tail load). The further the CP lies behind the CG, the larger that down-load. If the CG were behind the CP, the tail would need to lift upwards. 04.03.01.02

The IAS changes the balancing force. At low speed the wing works at a high CL, its centre of pressure is further forward and the tail needs less down-load; at high speed the CP moves aft and the camber moment, which grows with dynamic pressure, needs more. The balancing force is varied by changing the tail's angle of attack, through elevator deflection or by changing the stabiliser incidence (trim). The pilot or the trim system sets the deflection that gives the force needed for each speed and CG, and the tail force can be down or up. 04.03.01.03–04

Thrust also gives a pitching moment if its line of action does not pass through the CG. Engines below the CG, typically under-wing engines, pitch the nose up when thrust increases, so the elevator (or trim) must move nose-down; engines above the CG, such as tail-mounted engines high on the fuselage, pitch the nose down with more thrust and need nose-up elevator. 04.03.01.05

8.4 Static longitudinal stability and the CG

If a gust raises the nose, the angle of attack of both wing and tailplane increases. The wing's extra lift acts at its aerodynamic centre; the tail's extra lift acts far behind the CG with a long arm and pitches the nose back down. If the stabilising tail moment is larger than the destabilising wing moment, the aeroplane is statically stable in pitch.

That balance depends on the CG position. A forward CG gives a short wing arm and a long tail arm: more stability, but less manoeuvrability in pitch, with heavy forces and large elevator deflections needed. An aft CG gives less stability and more manoeuvrability, with light forces, until stability disappears. 04.03.02.01

8.5 The neutral point and static margin

The neutral point (NP) is the CG position at which the aeroplane would have neutral static longitudinal stability: the aerodynamic centre of the whole aeroplane, the point about which the total pitching moment does not change with angle of attack. 04.03.03.01

Its position depends only on the aerodynamic design: the wing's aerodynamic centre, the tail's size and arm, its lift-curve slope and the downwash, and the fuselage. Moving the load does not change it; moving the CG changes stability by changing the CG's distance from it. 04.03.03.02

The neutral point lies between the aerodynamic centre of the wing and that of the tailplane, normally a little behind the wing's AC. A larger tail or a longer tail arm moves it further aft. 04.03.04.01

So the aeroplane is stable as long as the CG is ahead of the neutral point; the further ahead, the more stable. With the CG at the neutral point it is neutrally stable, and behind it unstable. 04.03.05.01

The CG limits are set accordingly. 04.03.05.02

  • The forward limit is set by control: with the CG too far forward, the elevator may not have the power to rotate for take-off or to flare for landing, especially with flaps out and close to the ground, and control forces become very heavy. Elevator effectiveness, not stability, sets this limit. Stall speed and drag also rise.
  • The aft limit is set by stability: the CG must stay sufficiently ahead of the neutral point to keep positive stability and a minimum stick force per g, so that control forces do not become dangerously light.

The static margin is the distance between the CG and the neutral point, usually expressed as a percentage of the MAC. The larger it is, the more stable the aeroplane. 04.03.05.03

Exam trap. Forward CG limit: elevator authority (rotation and flare). Aft CG limit: stability. The neutral point does not move with loading; the CG does.

8.6 The Cm–α graph

The pitching-moment coefficient Cm (nose-up positive) plotted against angle of attack shows static stability directly. Where the line crosses Cm = 0 the aeroplane is trimmed. If the slope is negative, an increase in angle of attack gives a nose-down moment that restores it: stable. A steeper negative slope means more stability; a zero slope is neutral; a positive slope unstable. 04.03.06.01

The graph changes with: 04.03.07.01

  • CG shift: moving the CG aft makes the slope less negative (less stable), and at the neutral point the line is flat; moving it forward makes it steeper.
  • Elevator: moving the elevator up adds a nose-up moment and moves the whole line upwards without changing its slope, so it trims at a higher angle of attack (lower speed); elevator down moves it downwards.
  • Trim: moving the trim does the same as the elevator: it shifts the line up or down, setting the trimmed angle of attack, with no change of slope.
  • Wing contribution: with the CG ahead of the wing's AC, the wing is stabilising; behind it, destabilising. Its camber adds a constant nose-down moment, which moves the line down.
  • Tail contribution: strongly stabilising, a steep negative slope; it is what makes a conventional aeroplane stable.

8.7 Stick force stability

The pilot feels longitudinal stability through the control forces. In a stable aeroplane trimmed at a speed, flying slower needs a steady pull and flying faster a steady push, and releasing the column returns the aeroplane towards its trim speed. That is positive stick-force stability with speed. 04.03.10.01

The gradient of stick force with speed is steeper with a forward CG and shallower with an aft CG; at the same IAS it is broadly similar at different altitudes, because forces depend on dynamic pressure, though aeroelastic and Mach effects change it at high altitude. Changing the mass distribution so that the CG moves aft makes the forces lighter and the aeroplane feel less stable.

8.8 Stick force per g

The stick force per g is the pull needed to increase the load factor by 1 g, in a pull-up or a turn. In a stable aeroplane the stick force increases linearly with load factor. 04.03.12.01

It has a prescribed minimum and maximum. Too small a value lets the pilot overstress the aeroplane with a light pull; too large a value makes manoeuvring tiring and the aeroplane unresponsive. The stick force per g decreases with pressure altitude, because the aeroplane's natural pitch damping, which depends on air density, falls. 04.03.12.02

An aft CG reduces the stick force per g; at the manoeuvre point (slightly aft of the neutral point) it becomes zero. Trim does not change the stick force per g: the trimmed condition sets where the force is zero, but the gradient with g depends on the CG and the design. 04.03.14.01

8.9 Dynamic longitudinal stability

A disturbed aeroplane in pitch moves in two ways at once. 04.03.16.01

  • The phugoid (long-period oscillation): a slow exchange of speed and height at almost constant angle of attack. The nose drops, the aeroplane speeds up and descends, the extra lift makes it climb, it slows down, and the cycle repeats, with a period of around a minute or more. It is usually lightly damped, but so slow that the pilot corrects it easily.
  • The short-period oscillation: a rapid pitching, with large changes of angle of attack and load factor at nearly constant speed and height, with a period of a second or two. It is normally heavily damped and dies out within one or two cycles.

The short period is the more hazardous one, because it is fast. Its period is close to the pilot's reaction time, so control inputs can come too late and reinforce it instead of damping it, and its large changes of angle of attack and load factor can overstress the structure or stall the wing. 04.03.16.02

That reinforcement is a pilot-induced oscillation (PIO): oscillations in pitch (or roll) sustained or amplified by the pilot's own inputs, because each correction arrives too late and adds to the motion. The cure is to relax on the controls, or freeze them, and let the aeroplane's damping stop the motion. 04.03.16.03

At high altitude, the air's lower density reduces the aerodynamic damping that resists pitching (and rolling and yawing), so all the oscillations are less damped: dynamic stability is reduced. 04.03.16.04

Moving the CG aft reduces static stability and therefore the damping of the short-period motion, and makes the phugoid more lightly damped or unstable; at or behind the neutral point the motion diverges. A forward CG makes both better damped. 04.03.16.05

8.10 Directional stability

Static directional stability is the tendency of the aeroplane, after a disturbance in yaw, to return to flying with its nose into the relative airflow: it is weathercock stability. 04.04.01.01

Too weak, and the aeroplane wanders in yaw, is hard to keep straight and slips in turbulence; it may also be prone to Dutch roll. Too strong, combined with weak lateral stability, and it tends to the spiral dive (Section 8.13); it also makes crosswind landings harder, since the aeroplane wants to turn into wind. 04.04.01.02

The sideslip angle is the angle between the longitudinal axis and the relative airflow, seen from above: the aeroplane is flying partly sideways. 04.04.02.01 Its symbol is β (beta). 04.04.02.02

The yawing-moment coefficient Cn is the yawing moment about the normal axis, divided by the dynamic pressure, wing area and span. 04.04.03.01 For a directionally stable aeroplane, a sideslip produces a yawing moment that turns the nose into the relative wind, reducing the sideslip: Cn grows with β in the restoring sense. 04.04.03.02

On a Cn–β graph, Cn depends on β because a sideslip presents the fin and fuselage at an angle to the flow. Cn is zero at the β where the aeroplane is in equilibrium about the normal axis, and with no asymmetric thrust, control deflection or loading that β is zero. 04.04.04.01 The slope of the line measures static directional stability: the steeper the restoring slope, the more stable. 04.04.04.02 The slope is reduced at high altitude in the same IAS sense: at high Mach number the fin's lift-curve slope falls, and lower density reduces damping, so directional stability is less. 04.04.04.03

Many parts of the aeroplane contribute. 04.04.05.01

  • Wing: a small contribution; sweepback is stabilising, because in a sideslip the forward wing has more drag and pulls the nose back.
  • Fin: the main stabilising surface. In a sideslip it meets the air at an angle and produces a side force well behind the CG.
  • Dorsal fin: a fillet ahead of the fin that delays fin stall at large sideslip angles and adds side area aft.
  • Ventral fin: a fin under the rear fuselage that adds side area behind the CG, especially useful at high angles of attack when the main fin is blanketed.
  • Sweep of the fin: increases its arm behind the CG and its stalling sideslip angle.
  • Fuselage: the forward fuselage is destabilising; at high angles of attack, the forebody vortices can strongly change its contribution.
  • Strakes: on the forward fuselage or tail cone, they control the forebody vortices or add side area aft.

Moving the CG aft shortens the fin's arm and so reduces the directional stability (and the rudder's power). 04.04.05.02

8.11 Lateral stability

Static lateral stability is the tendency of the aeroplane, after a disturbance in roll, to return to wings level. 04.05.01.01 Strictly the aeroplane responds to the sideslip a bank causes, not to the bank itself.

Too weak, and the aeroplane drifts into a bank and turn after every gust. Too strong, and it rolls strongly in response to every sideslip, which makes crosswind handling harder, reduces roll response and promotes Dutch roll. 04.05.01.02

The bank angle φ (phi) is the angle between the lateral axis and the horizontal, measured about the longitudinal axis. 04.05.02.01

The rolling-moment coefficient Cl is the rolling moment about the longitudinal axis divided by the dynamic pressure, wing area and span. 04.05.03.01

Without coordination, a bank tilts the lift: its horizontal component pulls the aeroplane sideways towards the lower wing, so it slips sideways and a sideslip angle β appears, with the relative wind coming from the low side. 04.05.04.01

On the Cl–β graph, a laterally stable aeroplane produces, in a sideslip, a rolling moment that raises the lower (leading) wing. The curve passes through zero at zero sideslip, and its slope measures lateral stability: the steeper, the more stable. 04.05.05.01–02 As with directional stability, the effective slope falls at high altitude, because damping is lower and the aeroplane responds differently. 04.05.05.03

The contributions are: 04.05.06.01

  • Dihedral: in a sideslip, the forward (lower) wing meets the air at a higher angle of attack, gains lift and rolls the aeroplane level. Anhedral does the opposite and is destabilising.
  • High wing: in a sideslip, the fuselage blocks the crossflow, increasing the angle of attack of the forward wing's root, which is stabilising; together with a low CG, a high wing gives strong lateral stability (often balanced with anhedral). A low wing is destabilising and needs more dihedral.
  • Sweepback: in a sideslip the forward wing is effectively less swept, so it gives more lift, rolling the aeroplane level. Sweepback is strongly stabilising, more so at high CL; it often needs anhedral to stop it being too strong.
  • Ventral fin: lies below the roll axis, so its side force in a sideslip rolls the aeroplane the wrong way: destabilising.
  • Vertical tail (fin): lies above the roll axis, so its side force in a sideslip rolls the aeroplane level: stabilising.

8.12 Roll and yaw coupled

Lateral and directional stability are coupled. Any bank produces sideslip, and any sideslip produces both yaw (directional stability turns the nose into it) and roll (lateral stability rolls away from it). A yaw produces a speed difference between the wings and so roll; a roll produces sideslip and yaw. The two motions never happen alone. 04.06.02.01

8.13 Spiral divergence

If directional stability is strong and lateral stability weak, a small bank leads to a sideslip; the strong fin yaws the nose into it (into the turn) faster than the weak lateral stability can roll the wings level. The yaw speeds up the outer wing, which gains lift and steepens the bank. The bank and turn tighten, the nose drops, the speed increases and the aeroplane descends in a tightening spiral: spiral divergence (an unstable spiral mode). With the two in better balance the spiral is neutral (the bank stays constant) or stable (the wings slowly return level). 04.06.02.02

In an unstable spiral dive the speed increases, the bank angle increases, the nose drops further below the horizon and the aeroplane loses height at an increasing rate. It develops slowly, so it is dangerous mainly when the pilot is distracted or in cloud. Recovery: reduce power, roll the wings level first, then ease out of the dive. 04.06.02.03

8.14 Dutch roll

Dutch roll is a combined, oscillating yaw and roll, with the wing tips tracing ellipses as seen from behind: the aeroplane yaws one way and rolls the other way, repeatedly, with a period of a few seconds. 04.06.03.01

It happens when lateral stability is strong compared with directional stability. A yaw to the right makes the left wing go faster and gain lift, and the sideslip from the left rolls the aeroplane right strongly through the lateral stability. The sideslip then reverses, the fin yaws the aeroplane back, it overshoots, and the strong rolling reaction repeats. Swept wings, with strong lateral stability at high CL and weak fin damping at altitude, are especially prone. More directional stability and damping makes the oscillation stable (dying out); with less it becomes neutral or unstable (growing). 04.06.03.02

Airliners have a yaw damper: a system that senses the yaw rate and moves the rudder to oppose it automatically, damping the Dutch roll before it builds up. If the yaw damper is unavailable, the flight manual normally requires flying at a lower altitude and speed where natural damping is better. If a Dutch roll develops, the usual action is to damp it with small, well-timed aileron inputs against the roll (the rudder is generally not used, as mistimed inputs make it worse), or follow the type's procedure. 04.06.03.02

At high Mach numbers, a sideslip changes the effective sweep of the two wings: the shock wave is stronger on one wing than the other, changing the lift and drag on each side. That asymmetry adds a rolling and yawing moment that can start or worsen a Dutch roll. 04.06.03.03

8.15 Altitude and dynamic stability

Higher pressure altitude means lower air density and therefore less aerodynamic damping, while the aeroplane's inertia stays the same. The dynamic lateral and directional modes, especially Dutch roll, are therefore less damped at high altitude. 04.06.04.01

Check yourself

  1. An aeroplane tends to return after a disturbance but overshoots by more each time. Describe its stability. Statically stable, dynamically unstable (divergent oscillation).
  2. What sets the forward CG limit and what sets the aft limit? Forward: elevator authority for rotation and flare. Aft: stability.
  3. Define the static margin. The distance between the CG and the neutral point, as a % of MAC.
  4. What does moving the elevator up do to the Cm–α line? Moves it up without changing its slope, trimming at a higher angle of attack.
  5. What happens to stick force per g with an aft CG, and with altitude? It decreases in both cases.
  6. Which longitudinal mode is the more dangerous, and why? The short period: it is fast, near the pilot's reaction time, with large angle-of-attack and load-factor changes.
  7. Strong directional stability and weak lateral stability give which tendency? Spiral divergence.
  8. What does a ventral fin do to lateral stability? It reduces it (it lies below the roll axis).
  9. What is the function of a yaw damper? To damp Dutch roll by moving the rudder against the yaw rate.

chapters.label: Chapter 9
chapters.title: Control
chapters.html:
Stability keeps the aeroplane where it is; control makes it go somewhere else. Every primary control works the same way, by changing the camber and angle of attack of a surface so that it makes a force far from the CG. This chapter covers the controls about the three axes, the side effects of rolling and yawing, the tabs and powered systems that keep control forces manageable, fly-by-wire laws, and trim.

9.1 Axes, angles and controls

The aeroplane moves about three axes through its CG, each at right angles to the other two. 05.01.01.01

  • The lateral axis runs from wing tip to wing tip; motion about it is pitch.
  • The longitudinal axis runs from nose to tail; motion about it is roll.
  • The normal axis runs vertically through the CG, perpendicular to the other two; motion about it is yaw.

The pitch angle is the angle between the longitudinal axis and the horizontal; the bank angle (φ) the angle between the lateral axis and the horizontal; the yaw angle the angle between the longitudinal axis and a reference direction in the horizontal plane (such as the original heading). 05.01.01.02

Pitching moves the nose up and down, rolling lowers one wing and raises the other, and yawing swings the nose left and right. 05.01.01.03 The devices are the elevator (or all-moving tailplane) for pitch, the ailerons (helped by roll spoilers) for roll, and the rudder for yaw. 05.01.01.04

Deflecting a control surface changes the camber of the surface it belongs to. Moving a trailing-edge surface down adds positive camber and increases the lift; moving it up reduces or reverses the camber and decreases the lift. 05.01.02.01 At the same time it changes the local angle of attack: the chord line from leading edge to the deflected trailing edge is tilted, so a downward deflection increases the effective angle of attack of that section and an upward one reduces it. That is also why deflecting an aileron down near the stall can stall that wing. 05.01.03.01

9.2 Pitch control

The elevator is a hinged surface on the trailing edge of the tailplane. Moving it changes the tailplane's camber and lift; because the tail is far behind the CG, even a small force gives a large pitching moment. Pulling back raises the elevator, reduces the tail's lift (or increases its down-load) and pitches the nose up. An all-flying tail (stabilator) moves the whole tailplane, which is more powerful and stays effective at high Mach numbers, where a shock wave ahead of a hinged elevator would reduce its effect. 05.02.01.01

The tailplane sits in the downwash from the wing. Its angle of attack is therefore less than that of the aeroplane, by the downwash angle. Anything that changes the downwash, such as flap extension, a change of angle of attack or ground effect, changes the tail's angle of attack and so the pitching moment, which the pilot must trim out. 05.02.02.01

The CG position determines how much elevator is needed for a given response. With a forward CG, the tail arm is long but the aeroplane is very stable, so a larger elevator deflection (and force) is needed to change the attitude or load factor; with an aft CG, less. 05.02.04.01 The forward CG limit is therefore reached when the elevator, at full deflection, can only just achieve what is needed: rotation at take-off, and the flare at the landing speed with full flap in ground effect, where the downwash change makes the task hardest. 05.02.04.02

Engine thrust also pitches the aeroplane if its line of action misses the CG. Engines mounted low (under the wing) give a nose-up moment when thrust is increased and nose-down when it is reduced; engines mounted high (on the rear fuselage or above the wing) give the opposite. The effect is strongest at low speed with large thrust changes, such as a go-around. 05.02.05.01

9.3 Yaw control

The rudder is a hinged surface on the trailing edge of the fin. Deflecting it changes the fin's camber and side force, which, acting far behind the CG, yaws the aeroplane: the larger the deflection (and the dynamic pressure), the larger the yawing moment. Once the aeroplane yaws, it flies with sideslip; the fin, now meeting the air at an angle, produces a side force in the opposite sense, a restoring moment that balances the rudder at a steady sideslip angle. 05.03.01.01

At high speed a full rudder deflection would produce side loads beyond what the fin is built for. Transport aeroplanes therefore limit rudder travel as speed increases, with a ratio changer or travel limiter driven by airspeed, so that full pedal gives only a small deflection at high speed. Even so, large alternating rudder inputs (reversals) can overload the fin and must be avoided. 05.03.02.01

9.4 Roll control

The ailerons are hinged surfaces at the trailing edge of the outer wings, moving in opposite directions. The down aileron increases camber and lift on its wing, the up aileron reduces lift on the other, so the aeroplane rolls towards the up aileron. 05.04.01.01

Aileron deflection has adverse side effects: it causes adverse yaw (Section 9.6) and twists the wing, which at high speed can reduce or reverse its effect. 05.04.01.02

Many airliners have inboard and outboard ailerons. At low speed both are used for maximum roll power. At high speed the outboard ailerons, near the flexible tips, would produce large twisting loads, so only the stiffer, inboard ailerons are used. 05.04.01.03 The outboard ailerons are locked out above a given speed (or when the flaps are retracted) to prevent over-control, to avoid exceeding structural limits, and to avoid aeroelastic problems: flutter, divergence, and aileron reversal, in which the wing twists so much under the aileron's load that the change in angle of attack cancels or reverses the aileron's effect. 05.04.01.04

Ailerons are used: 05.04.01.05

  • in normal flight, to enter and leave turns and to hold the wings level;
  • in flight with sideslip, to hold the bank needed against the rolling moment that sideslip creates through lateral stability;
  • in crosswind landings, into wind, to stop the drift or to hold the wing down in the wing-low (sideslip) technique;
  • in horizontal turns, to roll in and out, with a small amount opposite to the turn sometimes needed to stop the bank increasing (overbanking);
  • with one engine inoperative, to hold a small bank towards the live engine and counter the rolling moment from asymmetric thrust and slipstream.

The roll rate is the angular velocity about the longitudinal axis, in degrees per second. 05.04.01.06 It depends on the aileron deflection and size, the dynamic pressure (IAS), the TAS (roll damping makes the steady roll rate proportional to TAS for a given aileron deflection), the span (a long wing has more roll damping and inertia), and aeroelastic wing twist. 05.04.01.07

Flaperons are surfaces that act as both flaps (moving down together) and ailerons (moving differentially). Aileron droop lowers both ailerons a little when the flaps are extended, so the whole trailing edge contributes extra lift. 05.04.01.08

9.5 Roll spoilers

Roll spoilers rise on the wing that must go down, reducing its lift (and adding drag on that side). They can work together with the ailerons or, at high speed when the outboard ailerons are locked out, partly replace them. They do not twist the wing as an aileron does, and their extra drag on the descending wing helps yaw the aeroplane into the turn. 05.04.03.01

9.6 Adverse yaw

The aileron going down increases its wing's lift and therefore its induced drag; the one going up reduces both. The extra drag on the rising wing pulls the nose away from the turn: adverse yaw. It is strongest at low speed and high CL. 05.04.04.01

It is reduced by: 05.04.05.01

  • Frise ailerons: the up-going aileron's nose projects below the wing into the airflow, adding drag on the descending wing to balance the down aileron's drag.
  • Differential aileron deflection: the up aileron moves further than the down one, increasing drag on the descending wing and limiting the induced drag of the rising wing.
  • Rudder–aileron cross-coupling: an interconnection that applies some rudder automatically with aileron.
  • Roll spoilers: they add drag on the descending wing, giving a favourable yaw.

9.7 Roll and yaw interaction

Rolling and yawing are coupled. 05.05.01.01–02

  • Secondary effect of roll: a bank makes the aeroplane slip towards the lower wing, and directional stability then yaws the nose towards the lower wing: rolling produces yaw.
  • Secondary effect of yaw: a yaw makes the outer wing move faster and gain lift (and the sideslip, through lateral stability, raises the leading wing's lift), so the aeroplane rolls in the direction of the yaw: yawing produces roll.

9.8 Reducing control forces: aerodynamic balance

The force on the pilot's controls is set by the hinge moment of the surface: its aerodynamic load times the arm about the hinge. On a large or fast aeroplane it would be too heavy to move by hand. Aerodynamic balance reduces the hinge moment by placing part of the surface's area or of the force ahead of the hinge, where the air helps the surface move. 05.06.01.01

  • A horn balance extends part of the surface, usually at its tip, ahead of the hinge line; the air pressure on it helps deflect the surface. 05.06.01.02
  • An internal balance places a flat plate ahead of the hinge inside a sealed chamber in the wing or tail; the pressure difference between the upper and lower surfaces acts on the plate and helps move the surface. 05.06.01.03

Tabs, small surfaces on the trailing edge of the control surface, also change the hinge moment. 05.06.01.04

  • A balance tab is geared to move opposite to the control surface. Its force helps move the surface and reduces the pilot's force.
  • An anti-balance tab is geared to move in the same direction, increasing the force. It is used to add feel to an over-light control, such as an all-moving tailplane.
  • A servo tab is moved directly by the pilot; its aerodynamic force moves the surface, which floats freely. The pilot only has to move the tab.
  • A spring tab is connected through a spring: at low speed the pilot moves the surface almost directly; at high speed, as loads build, the spring deflects and the tab helps more, like a servo tab.

9.9 Powered controls

With power-assisted controls, the pilot still moves the surface through a mechanical linkage, but hydraulic jacks add force; the pilot feels a fraction of the real aerodynamic load. With fully powered controls, the actuators move the surface entirely and the pilot feels no aerodynamic load at all: the control is irreversible. 05.06.02.01–02

Because a fully powered control gives no natural feel, an artificial feel system is added: springs and a feel unit that increases the force with dynamic pressure (q-feel). It gives the pilot a sense of speed and load, prevents over-controlling and overstressing, and keeps control forces similar to those of a well-designed manual aeroplane. 05.06.02.03

9.10 Fly-by-wire

In a fly-by-wire (FBW) aeroplane the controls send electrical signals to computers, which move the surfaces according to a control law.

In pitch, the side stick or column typically commands a load factor or pitch rate (or a blend) rather than an elevator deflection. With the stick released the aeroplane holds its flight path, and trims itself automatically, adjusting for speed, configuration and thrust changes. 05.07.01.01

The computers know the aeroplane's CG position (from fuel and loading data). They can then adjust the control gains so that the handling is the same at every CG, allow the aeroplane to be flown with an aft CG and smaller tail for lower drag (relaxed stability), and use the CG in protections and in fuel transfer to the tail. 05.07.01.02

If sensors or computers fail, the system reverts to degraded laws, such as an alternate law with fewer protections or a direct law, in which stick deflection maps directly to surface deflection, as in a conventional aeroplane, with manual trim. In the last resort a mechanical backup may remain. 05.07.01.03

Protections keep the aeroplane inside its envelope (angle of attack, load factor, pitch and bank attitude, overspeed). Hard protections cannot be overridden by the pilot: whatever the stick input, the aeroplane will not exceed the limit (the approach used by Airbus). Soft protections increase the stick force or give warnings near the limit, but the pilot can exceed the limit with extra force (the approach used by Boeing). 05.07.01.04

9.11 Trim

Trimming removes the steady control force needed to hold an attitude or speed, so that the pilot does not have to hold it. A change of speed, configuration, power or CG changes the balance of moments and therefore the force needed; trim cancels it, reducing fatigue and freeing the pilot to fly accurately. 05.08.01.01

The difference from balance tabs: a trim tab is set independently by the pilot (or autopilot) and stays in position, setting the zero-force condition; a balance tab moves automatically with the control surface and changes the force needed for each deflection, without changing the trimmed condition. 05.08.01.02

A trim tab is a small hinged surface on the elevator (or rudder or aileron) trailing edge, set from the cockpit with a wheel or switch. Moving the tab one way makes the control surface float the other way: to hold the elevator up (nose-up trim), the trim tab moves down. The flight deck indication shows the trim setting, for example a pointer marked nose-up and nose-down. 05.08.02.01

On jet transports the whole horizontal stabiliser is moved instead: a trimmable horizontal stabiliser (THS), driven by a motor and screwjack. The elevator then streamlines with it once trimmed. The stabiliser position appears on a trim indicator, often graduated in units or degrees, with a green band for take-off. 05.08.03.01

Compared with a trim tab, a stabiliser trim: 05.08.03.02

  • gives a much larger trim range, needed for big CG and speed ranges;
  • keeps the elevator streamlined, so less drag, and keeps its full travel available for control;
  • but is heavier and more complex, and a runaway or jammed stabiliser is far more serious, because it is a very powerful surface.

The take-off trim setting depends on the CG. A forward CG needs more nose-up stabiliser trim, so the rotation force is normal; an aft CG needs less. The setting is calculated from the load sheet's CG (and sometimes thrust and flap), and a take-off configuration warning sounds if it is outside the green band. 05.08.03.03

If the trim is set wrongly for take-off: 05.08.03.04

  • too nose-down (or the CG further aft than assumed): rotation needs a heavy pull and is slow, the lift-off is delayed and the take-off run longer;
  • too nose-up (or the CG further forward than assumed): the aeroplane rotates early or by itself, may over-rotate, risks a tail strike and lifts off at too low a speed.

A runaway stabiliser moves continuously, uncommanded, producing a rapidly growing out-of-trim force; it must be stopped at once with the trim cut-out switches, then trimmed manually if possible. A jammed stabiliser stays at one setting. 05.08.03.05 The consequences depend on where it jams. During take-off, jammed out of the green band, rotation forces are abnormal. On landing, jammed in a cruise setting, very large elevator forces are needed as the aeroplane slows and flaps are extended; the procedure usually calls for a higher approach speed, reduced flap and care in the flare. During a go-around, the thrust increase and configuration change produce large pitch changes the elevator alone may struggle to hold. 05.08.03.06

Check yourself

  1. Which axis is pitch about, and which control commands it? The lateral axis; the elevator or all-moving tail.
  2. Why is rudder travel limited at high speed? To avoid overloading the fin.
  3. Why are outboard ailerons locked out at high speed? To prevent over-control, overstress and aeroelastic effects such as flutter and aileron reversal.
  4. What causes adverse yaw? The extra induced drag of the down-going aileron's wing.
  5. How does a differential aileron reduce adverse yaw? The up aileron moves further than the down one, adding drag on the descending wing.
  6. Which tab moves in the same direction as its control surface, and why? The anti-balance tab, to increase the control force (add feel).
  7. To trim nose-up with a trim tab, which way does the tab move? Down.
  8. What is a hard protection? A FBW limit the pilot cannot exceed whatever the stick input.
  9. A forward CG at take-off needs which stabiliser setting? More nose-up trim.

chapters.label: Chapter 10
chapters.title: Limitations and Flight Envelopes
chapters.html:
Every aeroplane is certified for a limited range of speeds and loads. Above them the structure may bend permanently or fail, flutter may tear a surface off, or a flap or gear door may be damaged. This chapter explains the operating speed limits, the manoeuvring envelope (the V–n diagram) and the gust envelope, and what changes them.

10.1 Flutter

Flutter is a self-sustaining, rapidly growing oscillation of a structure, such as a wing, tailplane or control surface, in which aerodynamic forces and the structure's elastic and inertial properties feed one another. A wing bends, which changes its angle of attack, which changes the lift, which bends it further, while the inertia of a control surface or engine lags behind and adds energy each cycle. Above the flutter speed the oscillation grows until the structure fails, sometimes within seconds. The likelihood increases with IAS (dynamic pressure supplies the energy) and with an unfavourable mass distribution, especially when a surface's centre of mass lies behind its hinge line or elastic axis. 06.01.01.01

The cure is mass balance: placing mass so that the inertia works against the oscillation. 06.01.01.02

  • Wing-mounted engines on pylons are placed ahead of the wing's elastic axis, where their mass damps the coupling of bending and twisting.
  • Control surfaces have balance weights ahead of the hinge line, so that their centre of mass is on or ahead of the hinge, and the surface does not lag behind the wing's motion.

The aeroplane is designed and tested so that the whole flight envelope, up to the design dive speed VD/MD with a margin (typically 1.2 × VD), is free of flutter. Damaged balance weights, loose control surfaces, excess play or extra paint layers can lower the flutter speed into the normal envelope. 06.01.01.03

10.2 Gear and flap speeds

Landing gear and flaps are not designed to take the loads of high-speed flight. 06.01.03.01

  • VLO (landing gear operating speed) is the maximum speed at which the gear may be extended or retracted.
  • VLE (landing gear extended speed) is the maximum speed at which the aeroplane may be flown with the gear extended (and locked).

On some types VLO is lower than VLE, because during extension or retraction the gear doors are open and the gear is unlocked and moving, so it is more exposed to the airflow and its actuators and doors can only take lower loads than the locked, extended gear. 06.01.03.02

VFE (flaps extended speed) is the maximum speed with the flaps in a given extended position. Each flap setting has its own VFE, lower for larger flap settings, set by the structural strength of the flaps and their mechanism and by the larger loads the bigger deflections carry. 06.01.03.03

To prevent flap overload, aeroplanes use placards and VFE markings (the white arc on light aircraft), flap load relief systems that automatically retract the flaps to a smaller setting if the speed exceeds VFE and re-extend them when the speed drops, overspeed warnings, and procedures that require the speed to be below the next setting's VFE before selecting it. 06.01.03.04

10.3 Maximum speeds

06.01.04.01–02

  • VNO (maximum structural cruising speed, CS-23) is the speed that should not be exceeded except in smooth air, and then only with caution; it is the top of the green arc. It is set no higher than the design cruising speed VC.
  • VNE (never-exceed speed, CS-23) is the speed that must never be exceeded: the red line. It is set at no more than 0.9 VD, leaving a margin for inadvertent upsets.
  • VMO (maximum operating speed, CS-25 and turbine aeroplanes) is the maximum IAS that may not be deliberately exceeded in any phase of flight; it is no higher than VC, with a margin to VD for upsets.

They differ in what they protect: VNO marks the start of a caution range where gusts could overstress the structure; VNE and VMO are hard limits, chosen to keep a margin below the design dive speed, where flutter, control and structural problems could occur.

Flying above VNE or VMO risks: structural loads above limit, especially in gusts or manoeuvres; flutter and other aeroelastic effects; reduced or reversed control effectiveness; damage to doors, fairings and windscreens; and, close to VD, loss of the margin the designer built in. 06.01.04.03

MMO (maximum operating Mach number) is the Mach number that may not be deliberately exceeded. It is set by high-speed buffet and shock-induced separation, Mach tuck and changes in stability and control, flutter and aeroelastic margins, and the need to keep a margin below the design dive Mach number MD. 06.01.05.01

10.4 The manoeuvring-load (V–n) diagram

The manoeuvring-load diagram shows, for a given mass and configuration, the load factors the aeroplane can produce and withstand against equivalent airspeed. Its boundaries are the stall at the left (the most load factor the wing can produce at each speed), the limit load factors at the top and bottom, and the design dive speed at the right. Inside, the aeroplane can manoeuvre safely; outside, it either stalls or is overstressed. 06.02.01.01

The limit load factor is the largest load the aeroplane is expected to meet in service. The structure must carry it without permanent deformation. The ultimate load factor is the limit load times a safety factor of 1.5; the structure must carry it without failure for at least three seconds, but may be permanently deformed. Exceeding the limit load risks permanent bending of the structure; exceeding the ultimate load risks structural failure. 06.02.01.02

The design speeds are: 06.02.01.03

  • VA: the design manoeuvring speed, the speed at which the aeroplane stalls at its positive limit load factor.
  • VB: the design speed for maximum gust intensity, used for transport aeroplanes in turbulence.
  • VC: the design cruising speed.
  • VD: the design diving speed, the highest speed the structure is designed for.

On the diagram: 06.02.01.04

  • the vertical axis is the load factor n;
  • the horizontal axis is the speed, as EAS, so the diagram applies at any altitude (below where compressibility matters);
  • the outline is the EAS envelope: stall curves on the left, +limit and −limit horizontally, and VD on the right;
  • the 1-g stall speed VS1G is where the positive stall curve crosses n = 1;
  • the stall boundary follows n = (V / VS1G)², a parabola, rising to the positive limit at VA (and similarly for negative load factors with the negative CLMAX).

VMO or VNE lies between VC and VD: VMO no higher than VC for transport aeroplanes, VNE about 0.9 VD for light aeroplanes, leaving a margin for upsets. 06.02.01.05

Key numbers · limit load factors

Category Flaps up Flaps extended
CS-25 (large aeroplanes) +2.5 to −1.0 +2.0 to 0
CS-23 normal +3.8 to −1.52 +2.0 to 0
CS-23 utility +4.4 to −1.76 +2.0 to 0
CS-23 aerobatic +6.0 to −3.0 +2.0 to 0

For CS-25 the positive limit is 2.1 + 24 000 / (W + 10 000), W in lb, between 2.5 and 3.8; the negative limit of −1.0 applies up to VC and reduces to 0 at VD. 06.02.01.06

Since the stall speed at n is VS√n, the speed at which the aeroplane stalls exactly at its positive limit is VA = VS1G × √nlimit. 06.02.01.07

Worked example · VA. VS1G = 120 kt and n = 2.5: VA = 120 × √2.5 ≈ 190 kt. A CS-23 normal-category aeroplane with VS = 60 kt and n = 3.8: VA = 60 × √3.8 ≈ 117 kt.

Below VA, a full, abrupt nose-up elevator input will stall the wing before the limit load factor is reached, so the structure is protected by the stall. Above VA, the same input can produce a load factor above the limit, causing permanent deformation or failure, before the wing stalls. Full, abrupt deflection of a control is acceptable only below VA, and even then repeated or reversing inputs (especially of the rudder) can exceed the design loads. 06.02.01.08

10.5 Mass and altitude

The limit load factor is a load per unit weight. A heavier aeroplane at the same load factor puts a higher absolute load on the structure; the accelerated stall boundary moves to higher speeds with √mass. 06.02.02.01 Because VA = VS√n and VS changes with √mass, VA decreases at lower mass: VA2 = VA1 × √(m2 / m1). A light aeroplane reaches its limit load factor at a lower speed, because it stalls at a lower speed. 06.02.02.02

Worked example · VA and mass. VA = 110 kt at 1100 kg. At 880 kg: VA = 110 × √(880/1100) = 110 × 0.894 ≈ 98 kt.

At high altitude VA loses its meaning. There the stall IAS rises because of compressibility, high-speed buffet appears, and the envelope is bounded by Mach number limits rather than by the EAS-based V–n diagram; VA may lie close to or even above the maximum operating speed, and the useful protection comes from the buffet boundaries (Chapter 7). 06.02.02.03

MC is the design cruising Mach number and MD the design diving Mach number: the Mach equivalents of VC and VD that bound the envelope at high altitude. 06.02.02.04

10.6 The gust envelope

A vertical gust suddenly changes the wing's angle of attack and so its lift and load factor. The gust-load diagram shows, against EAS, the load factors produced by gusts of specified vertical speed: straight lines fanning out from n = 1 at zero speed, steeper for stronger gusts. The aeroplane must withstand them within the envelope. 06.03.01.01

Key numbers · design gusts (EAS)

At Gust m/s kt
VB 66 ft/s 20.1 39
VC 50 ft/s 15.2 30
VD 25 ft/s 7.6 15

These are the classic values used in the exam, applying up to 20 000 ft and reducing linearly above it. Modern CS-25 uses a refined discrete-gust method with similar reference values.

The rough-air speed VRA is the speed recommended for flight in turbulence. It is chosen to give a good margin against the stall and low-speed buffet in the strongest gusts, while staying far enough below VMO/MMO that speed excursions in turbulence will not exceed it, and no higher than VB. It is close to VB. 06.03.01.02

Turbulence causes structural loads (fatigue and possible overstress), speed and height excursions, stall or buffet if gusts raise the angle of attack, possible loss of control, difficulty reading instruments, and passenger and crew injuries. Fly at VRA, keep the attitude rather than chasing speed and height, and keep seat belts fastened. 06.03.01.03

10.7 What sets the gust load

The increase in load factor from a gust is approximately:

Δn = ρ0 × a × Ue × VE / (2 × W/S)

where ρ0 is sea-level density, a the lift-curve slope, Ue the equivalent gust speed and VE the EAS. So the gust load factor 06.03.02.01

  • increases with a steeper lift-curve slope: a higher aspect ratio makes it worse, more sweep (a flatter lift curve) better;
  • increases with EAS and with the speed of the vertical gust;
  • decreases with higher wing loading: a heavier aeroplane (or a smaller wing area) feels a smaller load factor from the same gust, and a light one is thrown around more;
  • in terms of altitude, at the same EAS it is unchanged by the formula, but at the same TAS the lower density at altitude reduces it.

Check yourself

  1. What makes flutter more likely, and what prevents it? Higher IAS and a centre of mass behind the hinge or elastic axis; prevented by mass balance ahead of the hinge.
  2. Why can VLO be lower than VLE? During transit the doors are open and the gear unlocked, so they can take less load.
  3. What is VNE in relation to VD? No more than 0.9 VD.
  4. What is the ultimate load factor of a CS-25 aeroplane with a limit of +2.5? +3.75 (1.5 × limit).
  5. VS1G 100 kt, limit +3.8. What is VA? About 195 kt.
  6. What happens to VA when the aeroplane is lighter? It decreases, with √mass.
  7. Which design gust applies at VC, in ft/s and kt? 50 ft/s, about 30 kt.
  8. Does a heavy or light aeroplane feel a larger load factor from the same gust? The light one (lower wing loading).

chapters.label: Chapter 11
chapters.title: Propellers
chapters.html:
A propeller is a set of rotating wings. Each blade section meets an airflow made of its own rotation and the aeroplane's forward speed, and its lift and drag become thrust and torque. This chapter builds that velocity triangle, explains fixed-pitch and constant-speed propellers, efficiency, what happens when an engine fails, and the side effects of a big spinning disc on the front of an aeroplane.

11.1 Thrust and torque

A blade element meets a relative airflow that combines the rotational speed of the blade (2π × radius × rpm) and the aeroplane's TAS. Its aerodynamic force can be split in two ways. Relative to that airflow, it has lift (perpendicular) and drag (parallel). Relative to the aeroplane, it has thrust, along the propeller axis, and a torque force in the plane of rotation, opposing the rotation; summed over all the blades, the torque force times its radius is the aerodynamic torque the engine must supply. 07.01.01.01

For a fixed-pitch propeller at constant rpm, as IAS increases the relative airflow comes more from ahead, the blade angle of attack falls and so do both thrust and aerodynamic torque; the engine then speeds up unless the throttle is reduced. As speed falls, thrust and torque rise, with the greatest static thrust at zero airspeed. 07.01.01.02

11.2 Blade geometry

At the reference section (often 75 % of the radius) the parts of the velocity triangle are: 07.01.02.01

  • the blade chord line, from the leading to the trailing edge of the section;
  • the rotational velocity vector, in the plane of rotation;
  • the TAS vector, along the axis;
  • the helix angle (advance angle), between the resulting relative airflow and the plane of rotation;
  • the blade angle (pitch angle), between the chord line and the plane of rotation;
  • the blade angle of attack, between the chord line and the relative airflow: blade angle − helix angle.

Geometric pitch is the distance the propeller would advance in one revolution at zero blade angle of attack (if it moved like a screw in a solid). Effective pitch is the distance it actually advances in one revolution. The difference is the propeller slip: it is what produces the blade angle of attack and the thrust.

A fine pitch means a small blade angle: good for take-off and climb at low speed and high rpm. A coarse pitch means a large blade angle: good for cruise at high speed and lower rpm. 07.01.02.02

11.3 Blade twist

Blade twist is the decrease of the blade angle from root to tip. 07.01.03.01 It is needed because the rotational speed increases with radius while the forward speed is the same, so the helix angle is large near the root and small near the tip. To give every section about the same, efficient angle of attack, the blade angle must be large at the root and small at the tip. 07.01.03.02

11.4 Types of propeller

07.01.04.01

  • Fixed pitch: the blade angle is fixed in manufacture.
  • Adjustable pitch or variable pitch (non-governing): the blade angle can be changed, on the ground or by the pilot in flight, but is not automatically controlled.
  • Variable pitch (governing), the constant-speed propeller: a governor changes the blade angle automatically to keep the rpm selected by the pilot.

A fixed-pitch propeller is simple, light, cheap and reliable, but efficient only near one speed; elsewhere its blade angle of attack is too high or too low. A constant-speed propeller keeps an efficient angle of attack over a wide range of speeds and lets the pilot choose rpm and power separately, at the price of weight, cost, complexity and maintenance, plus extra pilot workload. 07.01.04.02

A fixed-pitch propeller is chosen for its mission: a climb propeller has a fine pitch, giving good take-off and climb performance but over-speeding and poor efficiency at high cruise speed; a cruise propeller has a coarse pitch, giving good efficiency at cruise but poor take-off and climb. 07.01.04.03

For a fixed-pitch propeller at constant rpm, the blade angle of attack falls as airspeed rises, because the helix angle increases while the blade angle stays fixed. A variable-pitch propeller increases its blade angle as airspeed rises, keeping the angle of attack near its best value. 07.01.04.04

The forces on a rotating blade differ with the mode of operation. 07.01.04.05

  • Normal: positive blade angle of attack; the force gives forward thrust and a torque opposing rotation, which the engine overcomes.
  • Windmilling: the airflow drives the propeller. The blade angle of attack is negative, the aerodynamic force points backwards (drag) and its torque component drives the propeller round, turning a failed engine. This produces a large drag.
  • Feathered: the blade angle is about 90°, edge-on to the airflow. The blades produce almost no force, the propeller stops, and drag is minimal.
  • Reverse: the blade angle is negative. The blades push air forwards, giving reverse thrust for braking after landing.

At constant IAS, making the pitch coarser (a larger blade angle) increases the blade angle of attack, so thrust and torque increase; if the engine power is unchanged, the rpm falls. Making it finer does the opposite. A constant-speed unit uses this to hold rpm: if the rpm rises, it coarsens the pitch to absorb more torque. 07.01.04.06

11.5 Efficiency

Propeller efficiency is the useful thrust power divided by the shaft power from the engine: η = (thrust × TAS) / shaft power. 07.01.05.01

It is zero at zero TAS, because no work is done on the aeroplane even though there is plenty of static thrust. It rises with speed to a maximum, about 80–85 %, and falls again at high speed as the blade angle of attack becomes too small and the tips approach the speed of sound (compressibility losses). A fixed-pitch propeller reaches its peak at one speed only and falls off on either side; a constant-speed propeller follows the envelope of many fixed-pitch curves and stays near its peak over a wide range. 07.01.05.02

At a given TAS and rpm, increasing the blade angle increases the blade angle of attack and the thrust, up to the point where the blade stalls; beyond it thrust falls and drag rises. 07.01.05.03

11.6 Ice on the propeller

Ice on the blades changes their shape and roughness, reducing thrust and efficiency and increasing the power needed. Ice usually builds and sheds unevenly, causing imbalance and vibration; ice thrown off the blades can damage the fuselage, which is why fuselage panels next to propellers are reinforced. Propellers are protected by electrical de-icing boots or fluid systems. 07.01.06.01

11.7 Engine failure: windmilling and feathering

When an engine fails, its thrust is lost, and if its propeller windmills, it adds a large drag. On a twin, the remaining thrust on one side and the drag on the other produce a strong yawing moment towards the dead engine, which must be held with rudder, and the climb performance falls by much more than half. 07.02.01.01

Feathering turns the blades edge-on so the propeller stops and its drag is minimal. That reduces the yawing moment (so less rudder is needed and VMC is lower), improves performance (less drag, better climb), improves controllability, and prevents further damage to a failing engine. 07.02.02.01

11.8 Absorbing more power

A propeller must absorb the engine's power without excessive tip speed. Its ability to absorb power increases with: diameter, number of blades, blade chord (width), blade angle and camber, and rpm. 07.03.01.01

The diameter is limited by tip speed: the tips move fastest, and must stay well below the speed of sound to avoid compressibility losses and noise; and by ground clearance, especially at rotation and with a deflated tyre or compressed oleo, and clearance from the fuselage and the other propeller. 07.03.02.01

Solidity is the ratio of the total blade area to the area of the propeller disc. 07.03.03.01

More blades increase solidity and allow more power to be absorbed with a smaller diameter (lower tip speed and noise, better ground clearance), and give smoother running and less vibration. The disadvantages are more weight, cost and complexity, and a small loss of efficiency because each blade works in the disturbed air of the one ahead. 07.03.03.02

Propeller noise is reduced by lowering the tip speed (lower rpm or smaller diameter), using more blades, using swept or scimitar blade tips that delay compressibility at the tips, and synchronising or synchrophasing the propellers of multi-engine aeroplanes. 07.03.04.01

11.9 Torque, precession, slipstream and P-factor

Below, the propeller is assumed to turn clockwise as seen from the cockpit (from behind), as on most Western single-engine aeroplanes.

Torque reaction: by Newton's third law, as the engine turns the propeller clockwise, the propeller turns the aeroplane anticlockwise: it rolls to the left. On the ground this puts more load on the left wheel, adding to the swing; in the air it is trimmed out or held with aileron. 07.04.01.01

It can be cancelled by: 07.04.01.02

  • counter-rotating propellers: on a twin, the two engines turn in opposite directions, so their torques (and P-factors) cancel and there is no critical engine;
  • contra-rotating propellers: two propellers on the same axis turning in opposite directions, which cancels torque, gyroscopic effects and slipstream swirl.

Gyroscopic precession: a spinning propeller is a gyroscope. A force applied to its rim acts as if it were applied 90° further round in the direction of rotation. 07.04.02.01 Pitching or yawing the aeroplane therefore produces a moment about the other axis. With a clockwise propeller, pitching down (such as raising the tail of a tailwheel aeroplane on the take-off run) gives a yaw to the left; pitching up gives a yaw to the right; yawing left gives a pitch up, and yawing right a pitch down. The effect is strongest with large, heavy propellers and rapid attitude changes. 07.04.02.02

Slipstream: the air behind the propeller rotates in the same direction as the propeller, spiralling round the fuselage. With a clockwise propeller it strikes the left side of the fin and yaws the aeroplane to the left. The slipstream also blows faster air over the tail and inner wing, improving control and lift at low speed and with high power, and can cause asymmetric lift between the wings. 07.04.03.01

Asymmetric blade effect (P-factor): when the propeller axis is inclined to the flight path, at a high angle of attack in a climb or at low speed, the descending blade meets the air at a larger angle of attack and a higher speed than the ascending blade, so it produces more thrust. The centre of thrust moves towards the descending blade's side: with a clockwise propeller, to the right, yawing the aeroplane to the left. 07.04.04.01

On a twin with both propellers turning the same way (clockwise from behind), the descending blades are on the right of each engine. The right engine's thrust line therefore lies further from the centreline than the left's. If the left engine fails, the right engine's thrust acts with the longer arm and gives the greater yawing moment: the left engine is the critical engine. Slipstream effects over the fin can reinforce it. 07.04.04.02

11.10 Propeller effects in practice

With a clockwise propeller during the take-off run, torque loads the left wheel and the slipstream hits the left of the fin, both swinging the aeroplane left; on a tailwheel aeroplane, raising the tail adds a gyroscopic yaw to the left. At rotation and in the initial climb, P-factor at the high angle of attack adds further left yaw. The pilot holds the aeroplane straight with right rudder, more at high power and low speed. 07.04.05.01

In a go-around, full power is applied suddenly at low speed with the nose rising: torque, slipstream and P-factor all strengthen at once, producing a strong yaw and roll to the left (for a clockwise propeller) and a nose-up pitch, while the controls are least effective. Anticipate it with rudder and pitch control. 07.04.05.02

The go-around effects are made worse by: 07.04.05.03

  • high engine performance (low altitude, low temperature, high density): more thrust means more yaw, and on a multi-engine aeroplane higher VMC speeds;
  • loss of the critical engine during the go-around, which adds the largest asymmetric moment;
  • a crosswind, which, depending on its side, adds to or reduces the yaw through weathercocking;
  • a high flap setting, which leaves the aeroplane slow, with more drag and more slipstream effect over the flaps, while the rudder and ailerons are less effective.

Check yourself

  1. Blade angle 30°, helix angle 22°. What is the blade angle of attack? 8°.
  2. Why do blades have twist? Rotational speed increases towards the tip, so the blade angle must decrease to keep a similar angle of attack along the blade.
  3. Define propeller slip. The difference between the geometric and the effective pitch.
  4. What is the blade angle of attack of a windmilling propeller? Negative; the airflow drives the propeller and produces drag.
  5. Why is propeller efficiency zero at the start of the take-off run? Thrust power is thrust × TAS, and TAS is zero.
  6. Name two reasons for limiting propeller diameter. Tip speed (compressibility and noise) and ground clearance.
  7. With a clockwise propeller, which way does the aeroplane yaw when the tail is raised on a tailwheel aeroplane? Left (gyroscopic precession).
  8. On a twin with both propellers turning clockwise from behind, which engine is critical? The left engine.
