sections.title: 12.1 The four forces in level flight
12.8 Side forces and the hazards near VMC

chapters.html:
Flight mechanics applies Newton's laws to the four forces in each kind of steady flight: level, climbing, descending, gliding and turning. The same few formulas give climb gradients, glide range, turn radius and rate, and the load factor. The second half of the chapter deals with the most demanding steady case, flight with one engine inoperative, and the minimum control speeds that come from it.

12.1 The four forces in level flight

In straight, horizontal, steady flight the aeroplane is in equilibrium: no acceleration in any direction, so the forces balance. 08.01.01.01

The four forces are: 08.01.01.02

  • Lift, perpendicular to the flight path, acting through the wing's centre of pressure;
  • Weight, vertically downwards through the CG;
  • Thrust, along the thrust line of the engines;
  • Drag, parallel and opposite to the flight path, acting through a centre of drag.

Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag. Because the four forces do not all act through the same point, they also produce pitching moments: lift behind the CG pitches the nose down, thrust below the drag line pitches it up, and so on. The tailplane provides the extra (usually downward) force that brings the sum of the moments to zero, which means the wing must lift a little more than the weight. 08.01.01.03

12.2 The climb

The flight-path angle γ (gamma) is the angle between the flight path and the horizontal. 08.01.02.01 With no wind and no bank, the pitch attitude = γ + α: the nose is above the horizon by the climb angle plus the angle of attack. 08.01.02.02

In a straight, steady climb the weight no longer acts perpendicular to the flight path. Split along and across the path, it has a component W sin γ acting backwards along the path and W cos γ perpendicular to it. 08.01.02.03 Balancing the forces: 08.01.02.04

  • parallel to the path: T = D + W sin γ;
  • perpendicular to the path: L = W cos γ.

So in a climb thrust is greater than drag, because it must also lift part of the weight up the slope, 08.01.02.05 and lift is less than weight, because part of the weight is carried by the thrust. 08.01.02.06

For small angles sin γ ≈ γ (in radians) and lift ≈ weight, so

sin γ = (T − D) / W ≈ T/W − 1/(L/D)

The climb gradient depends on the excess thrust per unit of weight. 08.01.02.07

Worked example · climb gradient. Weight 500 kN, thrust 100 kN, L/D 12. Drag ≈ 500/12 ≈ 41.7 kN. sin γ = (100 − 41.7) / 500 = 0.117: a gradient of about 11.7 %, γ ≈ 6.7°. With the thrust halved (one engine of two), sin γ = (50 − 41.7)/500 = 0.017: 1.7 %. Losing half the thrust cut the gradient by about 86 %.

In a climb with constant vertical speed (such as autopilot V/S mode) and constant thrust setting, the thrust available falls as altitude increases, so the excess thrust falls. To keep the same rate of climb the aeroplane must use its kinetic energy: the IAS falls, the angle of attack rises, and the flight-path angle increases as TAS decreases (rate of climb = TAS × sin γ). Left alone, the speed decays towards the stall. 08.01.02.08

12.3 The descent

In a straight, steady powered descent, the weight component W sin γ now acts forwards along the path. 08.01.03.01 So: 08.01.03.02

  • parallel: T = D − W sin γ (with γ taken as the descent angle);
  • perpendicular: L = W cos γ.

Lift is less than weight, as in the climb, because the weight is tilted relative to the path. 08.01.03.03 Thrust is less than drag, because part of the weight helps pull the aeroplane along. 08.01.03.04

12.4 The glide

In a glide there is no thrust at all. 08.01.04.01 The forces are: 08.01.04.02

  • parallel: D = W sin γ;
  • perpendicular: L = W cos γ.

Dividing the two: tan γ = D / L. The glide angle depends only on the lift-to-drag ratio: the higher the L/D, the flatter the glide. The glide distance in still air is height × L/D. With wind, the air distance is unchanged but the ground distance is multiplied by GS / TAS. 08.01.04.03

Worked example · glide range. From 10 000 ft with L/D 12: still-air range = 10 000 × 12 = 120 000 ft ≈ 19.7 NM. Gliding at 120 kt TAS into a 20 kt headwind (GS 100 kt): 19.7 × 100/120 ≈ 16.4 NM.

VMD, the speed for minimum drag, is flown at the angle of attack that gives (L/D)max. It therefore gives the flattest glide and the greatest still-air glide distance. 08.01.04.04

Wind does not change the glide angle through the air, nor the time in the air (which depends on the rate of descent), but it changes the angle and distance over the ground. A headwind steepens the glide over the ground and shortens the distance; a tailwind flattens it and extends the distance. Duration is unchanged at the same airspeed. 08.01.04.05

Mass does not change (L/D)max. At VMD for each mass, a heavier aeroplane glides at the same angle and over the same distance, but VMD is higher (∝ √W), so it descends faster and the duration is shorter. If instead the heavier aeroplane keeps the same airspeed as the light one flew at its VMD, it is now below its own VMD, its L/D is lower, and it glides more steeply and less far. 08.01.04.06

Configuration changes reduce L/D: extending gear, flaps or speed brakes, or a windmilling propeller, makes the glide steeper and, at a given speed, increases the rate of descent, shortening the duration. 08.01.04.07

The rate of descent is TAS × sin γ. For the same gradient a higher TAS (higher altitude or higher weight) means a higher rate of descent. 08.01.04.08

VMP, the speed for minimum power required (power = drag × TAS), is lower than VMD, roughly 0.76 VMD. In a glide the power lost is W × rate of descent, so the minimum rate of descent is at VMP. It gives the longest time in the air, but not the longest distance, which is at VMD. 08.01.04.09

The pilot chooses between them. 08.01.04.10

  • Minimum glide angle (VMD), to reach the furthest point, such as a distant landing field after engine failure.
  • Minimum rate of descent (VMP), to stay airborne longest, for example to restart an engine or wait for help, or a glider in a thermal.

In a headwind, fly faster than VMD for the best range over the ground, because time in the wind is reduced; in a tailwind, slightly slower. In practice a speed a little above VMD is preferred anyway, because VMD and VMP lie in the region of neutral or negative speed stability, where speed is hard to hold.

12.5 The level turn

In a steady, coordinated turn the lift is tilted by the bank angle φ. Its vertical component, L cos φ, balances the weight; its horizontal component, L sin φ, provides the centripetal force that turns the aeroplane, m V² / R. 08.01.05.01

Dividing the two: tan φ = V² / (g R). 08.01.05.02

A coordinated turn has no sideslip: the ball of the slip indicator is centred. In a slipping turn the aeroplane has too much bank for its rate of turn (or too little rudder) and slips inwards: the ball moves to the inside of the turn. In a skidding turn it has too little bank for its rate of turn (too much rudder) and skids outwards: the ball moves to the outside. Correct either with rudder towards the ball ("step on the ball"), or by adjusting the bank. 08.01.05.03

The formula tan φ = V²/(gR) contains no mass. For a given TAS and radius, every aeroplane needs the same bank angle, light or heavy: the extra lift needed for a heavier aeroplane comes from a higher CL, not more bank. 08.01.05.04 And for a given bank, the radius depends only on TAS: R = V² / (g tan φ). 08.01.05.05

Worked example · turn radius. TAS 200 kt = 102.9 m/s, bank 30°: R = 102.9² / (9.81 × 0.577) ≈ 1870 m ≈ 1.0 NM. At 250 kt the same bank gives about 1.6 NM: the radius grows with the square of TAS. 08.01.05.06

Increasing the bank angle in a level turn has these effects. 08.01.05.07

  • The load factor n = 1 / cos φ rises: 1.15 at 30°, 1.41 at 45°, 2 at 60°.
  • The angle of attack must rise (more CL for more lift) at the same speed.
  • The drag rises, mainly induced drag, which grows with n².
  • So the thrust needed rises, or the aeroplane slows down.

The angular velocity is the rate at which an angle changes, in degrees or radians per second. 08.01.05.08 The rate of turn is the angular velocity of the heading change: ω = V / R = g tan φ / V. A rate-1 turn is 3° per second, a full 360° in 2 minutes. 08.01.05.09

At a given bank angle, a higher TAS gives a lower rate of turn and a larger radius. To keep rate 1, the bank needed increases with TAS; a useful approximation is bank ≈ TAS (kt) / 10 + 7. 08.01.05.10

Worked example · rate-1 bank. At 150 kt: bank ≈ 15 + 7 = 22°. At 250 kt: bank ≈ 32°, close to the 25–30° limit used in instrument flying.

The load factor and stall speed in a turn are n = 1/cos φ and VS turn = VS1G × √n. 08.01.05.11

Worked example · stall in a turn. VS1G = 140 kt, bank 45°: n = 1.41 and VS = 140 × 1.19 ≈ 166 kt.

Turn radius matters wherever protected airspace is designed around a speed. Departure and arrival procedures carry maximum IAS limits, and approach procedures use speed categories (A to E), because the obstacle-protected areas are sized for the radius of turn at that speed. Flying faster than the published speed makes the turn wider than the protected area, risking obstacles, terrain or other traffic, especially at high-altitude airports where the TAS for a given IAS is higher. 08.01.05.12

Using the rudder to tighten a turn in a swept-wing aeroplane is hazardous. The yaw creates sideslip, and the swept wing's strong lateral stability turns it into a powerful roll, which can quickly steepen the bank beyond control; large or reversing rudder inputs can also overload the fin. Turns are made with aileron and coordinated with the minimum rudder. 08.01.05.13

12.6 Asymmetric thrust

When an engine fails on a multi-engine aeroplane, the thrust of the remaining engine(s) and the drag of the failed one act on opposite sides of the CG. The aeroplane yaws towards the dead engine; the yaw speeds up the live engine's wing, and the loss of slipstream (on propeller aeroplanes) reduces lift on the dead side, so it also rolls towards the dead engine. Without correction it enters a spiral. The total drag increases (windmilling, sideslip, control deflections), and climb performance falls by far more than the proportion of thrust lost. On propeller aeroplanes the loss of slipstream over the wing and asymmetric propeller effects make it worse than on jets. 08.02.01.01

The critical engine is the engine whose failure has the most adverse effect on handling and performance. On a propeller twin with both propellers turning clockwise (from behind), it is the left engine, because P-factor moves the right engine's thrust line outboard (Chapter 11). On a jet with both engines identical, there is in principle no critical engine, though a crosswind or other asymmetries may define one. 08.02.01.02

With asymmetric thrust in steady flight, a conventional slip indicator does not show sideslip directly. In the wings-level method, with rudder alone holding the heading, the ball is centred but the aeroplane flies with sideslip towards the dead engine. In the wings-down method, with about 5° of bank towards the live engine and less rudder, the sideslip is zero but the ball lies about half a ball's width towards the live engine. 08.02.01.03

A crosswind adds a weathercocking yaw into wind. A crosswind from the side of the dead engine adds to the yaw towards it and demands more rudder; one from the live side helps. On the ground this directly affects the minimum control speed. 08.02.01.04

12.7 Balancing the yawing moments

About the CG, the yawing moments are: the live engine's thrust times its distance from the CG, plus the failed engine's drag (windmilling or not) times its distance; opposed by the rudder and fin side force times the fin's arm, and any sideslip moments. 08.02.02.01

The thrust depends on air density. At low altitude and low temperature (high density) the live engine gives more thrust and so more yawing moment; at high altitude or high temperature, less. 08.02.02.02

The further the engines are from the CG (wide-spaced wing engines), the larger the arm and the larger the yawing moment; engines close to the fuselage (rear-mounted jets) give a smaller moment. 08.02.02.03

To restore directional balance after an engine failure: 08.02.02.04

  • apply rudder against the yaw (towards the live engine);
  • bank slightly (up to 5°) towards the live engine to remove the sideslip;
  • feather the propeller (or reduce the windmilling drag);
  • if necessary, reduce thrust on the live engine;
  • keep speed up, because the rudder's power grows with dynamic pressure.

12.8 Side forces and the hazards near VMC

To hold a heading, the side forces must also balance. 08.02.03.01

  • The fin and rudder produce a side force that holds the yaw, pushing the tail towards the dead-engine side.
  • In the wings-level method, this side force is balanced by a fuselage side force from sideslip: the aeroplane flies with its relative wind from the dead-engine side. The sideslip changes the fin's angle of attack against the rudder, so more rudder is needed and drag is higher.
  • In the wings-down method, a bank of up to 5° towards the live engine tilts the lift vector, and its horizontal component balances the fin force with no sideslip. Less rudder is needed, drag is lower, and VMC is lower.

Flying near VMC brings several hazards. 08.02.03.02 The angle of attack is high at low speed, close to the stall, and a stall with asymmetric thrust can lead to a spin. The sideslip adds drag and, in the wrong sense, makes control harder. The fin works with full rudder at high loads, and its angle of attack, increased by sideslip and rudder deflection, can approach the fin stall, after which directional control is lost suddenly.

A sideslip changes the angle at which the air meets the fin. In the wings-level case, the sideslip from the dead-engine side gives the fin an angle of attack against the rudder's force, so the rudder must be deflected further for the same side force. A sideslip in the opposite sense, for example from too much bank towards the live engine, adds to the fin's angle of attack and, with full rudder, takes it towards the fin stall. 08.02.03.03

12.9 Mass and minimum control speeds

The rudder's power depends on dynamic pressure, so on speed, while the asymmetric thrust depends on the engines, not on mass. A light aeroplane has low stall speeds and so low take-off and approach speeds; at those speeds the rudder may not be able to balance full asymmetric thrust. Controllability with one engine inoperative is therefore a typical problem at low mass, and the minimum control speeds may limit the take-off speeds (V1, VR, V2) instead of the stall. 08.02.04.01

12.10 VMC, VMCL and VMCG

VMC (minimum control speed in flight, also VMCA) is the calibrated airspeed at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, it is still possible to maintain control of the aeroplane and to maintain straight flight with a bank angle of not more than 5° towards the live engine. 08.02.08.01

It is determined in flight test with: maximum available take-off thrust on the operating engine(s); the most unfavourable (normally the aft) CG; the aeroplane trimmed for take-off; take-off flaps; gear retracted; the propeller of the failed engine in the condition it would normally reach (windmilling, or feathered if automatic); out of ground effect; and at the most critical weight. The rudder force must not exceed 150 lbf (667 N), the heading change must stay within about 20°, and VMC may not exceed 1.13 VSR. 08.02.08.02

An aft CG shortens the arm between the CG and the rudder, so the rudder produces less yawing moment and VMC is higher. That is why VMC is determined at the aft limit. 08.02.08.03

VMCL (minimum control speed during approach and landing) is the calibrated airspeed at which, with the critical engine suddenly inoperative in the approach and landing configuration, control can be maintained and straight flight held with not more than 5° of bank. 08.02.09.01 It is determined with the aeroplane in the landing configuration, trimmed for approach, go-around thrust on the operating engine(s), the failed engine's propeller in its normal condition, the most unfavourable weight and aft CG, again with rudder force limits. 08.02.09.02 As for VMC, an aft CG gives a higher VMCL. 08.02.09.03

VMCG (minimum control speed on the ground) is the calibrated airspeed during the take-off run at which, when the critical engine is suddenly made inoperative, control can be maintained using the primary aerodynamic controls alone (no nosewheel steering) so that the take-off can safely continue, with the aeroplane deviating no more than 30 ft (9.1 m) laterally from the centreline. 08.02.10.01 It is determined with take-off thrust on the operating engine(s), the most critical take-off configuration, the aeroplane trimmed for take-off, the most unfavourable (aft) CG and weight, and a rudder force limit of 150 lbf. V1 may not be less than VMCG. 08.02.10.02 An aft CG again gives the shortest rudder arm and so the highest VMCG. 08.02.10.03

12.11 Density and minimum control speeds

The thrust of the live engine depends on air density: it is highest at low pressure altitude and low temperature. 08.02.11.01 The minimum control speeds are set by the balance between the asymmetric thrust and the rudder's power. Less thrust means less yawing moment, which the rudder can balance at a lower dynamic pressure, so VMC, VMCL and VMCG all decrease when thrust is reduced, at high altitudes and temperatures, or with derated take-off thrust. That is why the published values are highest at low, cold airfields. 08.02.11.02

12.12 Significant points on the polar

The aeroplane's polar curve (CL against CD) has several significant points. 08.03.01.01

  • CL = 0: the zero-lift point, giving the minimum value of drag coefficient close to it (CDmin).
  • The tangent from the origin: (CL/CD)max, the angle of attack for VMD, the best glide angle and, for a jet, maximum endurance.
  • The point of (CL^(3/2)/CD)max, at a higher CL: the angle of attack for VMP, minimum power and minimum rate of descent (and, for a propeller aeroplane, maximum endurance).
  • The point of (CL^(1/2)/CD)max, at a lower CL: the angle of attack for the jet's best range speed (about 1.32 VMD).
  • CLMAX: the top of the curve, the stall.

Check yourself

  1. Give the force equations for a steady climb. T = D + W sin γ; L = W cos γ.
  2. Why is lift less than weight in a climb? Part of the weight is carried by the thrust component along the path.
  3. An aeroplane with L/D 15 glides from 6000 ft in still air. How far does it go? 90 000 ft, about 14.8 NM.
  4. A heavier aeroplane glides at its own VMD. What changes? Same angle and distance; higher speed, higher rate of descent, shorter duration.
  5. At which speed is the minimum rate of descent in a glide? VMP.
  6. TAS 300 kt, 25° of bank. What is the radius of turn? About 5200 m, about 2.8 NM.
  7. Does the bank angle needed for a given radius and TAS depend on mass? No.
  8. With a 5° bank towards the live engine at zero sideslip, where is the ball? About half a width towards the live engine.
  9. Why does an aft CG increase VMC? It shortens the rudder's arm about the CG.
  10. How do VMC speeds change at a hot, high airfield? They decrease, because the live engine gives less thrust.
